allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 1 In patients with suspected acute stroke, does pre-hospital blood pressure lowering with any drug, compared to no drug, improve outcome?
allPracticeChanges.category: 2025 ESO Guideline on Blood Pressure Management in Acute Ischaemic Stroke and Intracerebral Haemorrhage
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with suspected stroke, we suggest against routine blood pressure lowering in the pre-hospital setting.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Strong against intervention (Evidence: Moderate, Voting: Vote: 10/10)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In patients with suspected acute stroke, does pre-hospital blood pressure lowering with any drug, compared to no drug, improve outcome?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: Due to the potential harm to patients with ICH, treatment with transdermal glyceryl trinitrate should be avoided. Intravenous urapidil or labetalol could be the treatment of choice.

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 2 In hospitalised patients with acute ischaemic stroke not treated with reperfusion therapies (intravenous thrombolysis or mechanical thrombectomy), does blood pressure lowering with any vasodepressor drug, compared to no drug, improve outcome?
allPracticeChanges.category: 2025 ESO Guideline on Blood Pressure Management in Acute Ischaemic Stroke and Intracerebral Haemorrhage
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In hospitalised patients with acute ischaemic stroke and blood pressure < 220/110 mmHg not treated with intravenous thrombolysis or mechanical thrombectomy, we suggest against the routine use of blood pressure-lowering agents at least in the first 24 h following symptom onset, unless this is necessary for a specific comorbid condition that requires blood pressure lowering.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Weak against intervention (Evidence: Moderate, Voting: Vote: 10/10)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In hospitalised patients with acute ischaemic stroke not treated with reperfusion therapies (intravenous thrombolysis or mechanical thrombectomy), does blood pressure lowering with any vasodepressor drug, compared to no drug, improve outcome?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: In hospitalised patients with acute ischaemic stroke and blood pressure > 220/120 mmHg not treated with intravenous thrombolysis or mechanical thrombectomy, careful blood pressure reduction (<15% systolic blood pressure reduction in 24 h) is reasonable and likely to be safe. No specific blood pressure-lowering agent can be recommended.

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 3 In hospitalised patients with acute ischaemic stroke and undergoing intravenous thrombolysis (with or without mechanical thrombectomy), do blood pressure-lowering therapies compared to control improve outcome?
allPracticeChanges.category: 2025 ESO Guideline on Blood Pressure Management in Acute Ischaemic Stroke and Intracerebral Haemorrhage
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In hospitalised patients with acute ischaemic stroke and undergoing intravenous thrombolysis (with or without mechanical thrombectomy), we suggest maintaining blood pressure below 185/110 mmHg before bolus, and below 180/105 mmHg after bolus and for 24 h. No specific blood pressure-lowering agent can be recommended.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Weak for intervention (Evidence: Very low)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In hospitalised patients with acute ischaemic stroke and undergoing intravenous thrombolysis (with or without mechanical thrombectomy), do blood pressure-lowering therapies compared to control improve outcome?

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 3 In hospitalised patients with acute ischaemic stroke and undergoing intravenous thrombolysis (with or without mechanical thrombectomy), do blood pressure-lowering therapies compared to control improve outcome?
allPracticeChanges.category: 2025 ESO Guideline on Blood Pressure Management in Acute Ischaemic Stroke and Intracerebral Haemorrhage
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In hospitalised patients with acute ischaemic stroke and undergoing intravenous thrombolysis (with or without mechanical thrombectomy), we suggest against lowering systolic blood pressure to a target of 130–140 mmHg compared to < 180 mmHg during the first 72 h following symptom onset.
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In hospitalised patients with acute ischaemic stroke and undergoing intravenous thrombolysis (with or without mechanical thrombectomy), do blood pressure-lowering therapies compared to control improve outcome?

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 4 In patients with acute ischaemic stroke caused by LVO and undergoing mechanical thrombectomy (with or without intravenous thrombolysis), does blood pressure lowering with any vasodepressor drug compared to no drug improve functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.category: 2025 ESO Guideline on Blood Pressure Management in Acute Ischaemic Stroke and Intracerebral Haemorrhage
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke caused by LVO and undergoing mechanical thrombectomy (with or without intravenous thrombolysis), we suggest keeping blood pressure below 180/105 mmHg during, and for 24 h after, mechanical thrombectomy. No specific blood pressure-lowering agent can be recommended.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Weak against intervention (Evidence: Very low)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke caused by LVO and undergoing mechanical thrombectomy (with or without intravenous thrombolysis), does blood pressure lowering with any vasodepressor drug compared to no drug improve functional outcome?

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 4 In patients with acute ischaemic stroke caused by LVO and undergoing mechanical thrombectomy (with or without intravenous thrombolysis), does blood pressure lowering with any vasodepressor drug compared to no drug improve functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.category: 2025 ESO Guideline on Blood Pressure Management in Acute Ischaemic Stroke and Intracerebral Haemorrhage
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke caused by LVO and undergoing mechanical thrombectomy (with or without intravenous thrombolysis), we suggest against individualised blood pressure management (guided by pre-procedural blood pressure levels) during mechanical thrombectomy.
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke caused by LVO and undergoing mechanical thrombectomy (with or without intravenous thrombolysis), does blood pressure lowering with any vasodepressor drug compared to no drug improve functional outcome?

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 4 In patients with acute ischaemic stroke caused by LVO and undergoing mechanical thrombectomy (with or without intravenous thrombolysis), does blood pressure lowering with any vasodepressor drug compared to no drug improve functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.category: 2025 ESO Guideline on Blood Pressure Management in Acute Ischaemic Stroke and Intracerebral Haemorrhage
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke caused by LVO and undergoing mechanical thrombectomy (with or without intravenous thrombolysis), we recommend against actively reducing systolic blood pressure < 140 mmHg for the first 24 h following successful mechanical thrombectomy.
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke caused by LVO and undergoing mechanical thrombectomy (with or without intravenous thrombolysis), does blood pressure lowering with any vasodepressor drug compared to no drug improve functional outcome?

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 4 In patients with acute ischaemic stroke caused by LVO and undergoing mechanical thrombectomy (with or without intravenous thrombolysis), does blood pressure lowering with any vasodepressor drug compared to no drug improve functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.category: 2025 ESO Guideline on Blood Pressure Management in Acute Ischaemic Stroke and Intracerebral Haemorrhage
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke caused by LVO and undergoing mechanical thrombectomy (with or without intravenous thrombolysis), systolic blood pressure drops should be avoided.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Strong against intervention (Evidence: Very low)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke caused by LVO and undergoing mechanical thrombectomy (with or without intravenous thrombolysis), does blood pressure lowering with any vasodepressor drug compared to no drug improve functional outcome?

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 5 In patients with acute ischaemic stroke not treated with reperfusion therapies (intravenous thrombolysis or mechanical thrombectomy) and with clinical deterioration, does induced hypertension by any vasopressor drug compared to no drug improve outcome?
allPracticeChanges.category: 2025 ESO Guideline on Blood Pressure Management in Acute Ischaemic Stroke and Intracerebral Haemorrhage
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke not treated with reperfusion therapies (intravenous thrombolysis or mechanical thrombectomy) and with clinical deterioration, we suggest against the routine use of vasopressor drugs to increase blood pressure.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Weak against intervention (Evidence: Very low, Voting: Vote: 10/10)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke not treated with reperfusion therapies (intravenous thrombolysis or mechanical thrombectomy) and with clinical deterioration, does induced hypertension by any vasopressor drug compared to no drug improve outcome?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke not treated with reperfusion therapies (IVT or MT) and with clinical deterioration where a haemodynamic mechanism is suspected or shown to be directly responsible for the deterioration, we suggest: • Stopping existing BP lowering therapy, • Administering intravenous fluids and • Introducing non-pharmacological procedures to raise BP Before considering • Careful use of vasopressor agents to increase BP with close monitoring of BP values.

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 6 In patients with acute ischaemic stroke, does continuing vs temporarily stopping previous oral blood pressure-lowering therapy improve outcome?
allPracticeChanges.category: 2025 ESO Guideline on Blood Pressure Management in Acute Ischaemic Stroke and Intracerebral Haemorrhage
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke, we suggest against routinely continuing previous oral blood pressure-lowering therapy.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Weak against intervention (Evidence: Low, Voting: Vote: 10/10)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke, does continuing vs temporarily stopping previous oral blood pressure-lowering therapy improve outcome?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke, we suggest stopping previous oral blood pressure-lowering therapy in patients with dysphagia until swallowing is restored or a nasogastric tube is in place.

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 7 In patients with acute ICH, does intensive blood pressure lowering with any vasodepressor drug compared to control improve outcome?
allPracticeChanges.category: 2025 ESO Guideline on Blood Pressure Management in Acute Ischaemic Stroke and Intracerebral Haemorrhage
allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with acute spontaneous ICH and systolic blood pressure of 150–220 mmHg, the overall balance of beneficial and adverse effects is uncertain, so we recommend recruitment to ongoing randomised controlled trials.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Uncertain / Ongoing trials (Evidence: Moderate, Voting: Vote: 10/10)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In patients with acute ICH, does intensive blood pressure lowering with any vasodepressor drug compared to control improve outcome?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement:
1. We suggest lowering systolic blood pressure below 140 mmHg within 6 h of symptom onset in minor or moderate ICH (haematoma volume < 30 mL) to reduce haematoma expansion (Vote: 10/10).
2. For patients with spontaneous ICH, we suggest avoiding a reduction in SBP of more than 70 mmHg from baseline and avoiding active reduction of SBP below 110 mmHg. Caution is advised when lowering very high SBP (>220 mmHg), in patients with large haematoma volumes (>30 mL) or when haematoma evacuation is planned (Vote: 10/10).
3. In patients with acute ICH, blood pressure target-based interventions should be preferred over interventions based on fixed antihypertensive agents (Vote: 10/10).
4. For patients with spontaneous minor or moderate ICH (<30 mL): In acute phase (<2 h), lower SBP to <140 mmHg and minimise variability. In sub-acute phase (up to 7 days), maintain SBP below 140 mmHg (Vote: 10/10).

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 8 In patients with acute ICH, does continuing vs temporarily stopping previous oral antihypertensive therapy improve outcome?
allPracticeChanges.category: 2025 ESO Guideline on Blood Pressure Management in Acute Ischaemic Stroke and Intracerebral Haemorrhage
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with acute ICH there is continued uncertainty over the benefits and risks (advantages/disadvantages) of continuing vs temporarily stopping previous blood pressure-lowering therapy.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Uncertain / Ongoing trials (Evidence: Moderate, Voting: Vote: 10/10)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In patients with acute ICH, does continuing vs temporarily stopping previous oral antihypertensive therapy improve outcome?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement:
1. In patients with acute ICH who need BP-lowering therapy to maintain BP within the recommended range and who do not have swallowing difficulties, we suggest continuation of prior oral antihypertensive agents (Vote: 10/10).
2. In patients with acute ICH who need BP-lowering therapy and who have dysphagia or decreased level of consciousness, we suggest temporarily stopping previous oral hypertensive therapy and using intravenous antihypertensive agents until swallowing is restored or a nasogastric tube is in place (Vote: 10/10).

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 1: 1: Organised Stroke Unit Care In adults with spontaneous ICH, does admission to an organised stroke unit versus admission to a general ward reduce the risk of death or death/dependence?
allPracticeChanges.category: 1: Organised Stroke Unit Care In adults with spontaneous ICH
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In adults with spontaneous ICH, not requiring intensive care treatment, we recommend admission to an organised stroke unit to reduce the risk of death or dependence.
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: 1: Organised Stroke Unit Care In adults with spontaneous ICH, does admission to an organised stroke unit versus admission to a general ward reduce the risk of death or death/dependence?

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 1: 1: Organised Stroke Unit Care In adults with spontaneous ICH, does admission to an organised stroke unit versus admission to a general ward reduce the risk of death or death/dependence?
allPracticeChanges.category: 1: Organised Stroke Unit Care In adults with spontaneous ICH
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In adults with spontaneous ICH, we suggest using algorithms such as DIAGRAM for targeted investigation of ICH cause versus standard care to improve the performance (calibration/discrimination/clinical utility) of prediction of underlying cause of ICH.
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: 1: Organised Stroke Unit Care In adults with spontaneous ICH, does admission to an organised stroke unit versus admission to a general ward reduce the risk of death or death/dependence?

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 1: 1: Organised Stroke Unit Care In adults with spontaneous ICH, does admission to an organised stroke unit versus admission to a general ward reduce the risk of death or death/dependence?

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In adults with spontaneous ICH there is uncertainty about whether cerebral computed tomographic angiography (CTA) / venography (CTV), or magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) / venography (MRV) have superior diagnostic performance when compared with intraarterial digital subtraction angiography (IADSA) to disclose underlying intracranial vascular malformations, so we recommend recruitment to diagnostic test accuracy studies.
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: 1: Organised Stroke Unit Care In adults with spontaneous ICH, does admission to an organised stroke unit versus admission to a general ward reduce the risk of death or death/dependence?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: In adults with spontaneous ICH, we suggest using cerebral computed tomographic angiography (CTA)/venography (CTV), or magnetic resonance angiography (MRA)/venography (MRV) to select patients for intra-arterial digital subtraction angiography (IADSA) to disclose underlying intracranial vascular malformations.

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 1: 1: Organised Stroke Unit Care In adults with spontaneous ICH, does admission to an organised stroke unit versus admission to a general ward reduce the risk of death or death/dependence?
allPracticeChanges.category: 1: Organised Stroke Unit Care In adults with spontaneous ICH
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In adults with ICH, there is continued uncertainty whether outcome prediction tools have better predictive properties compared with clinicians' evaluation.
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: 1: Organised Stroke Unit Care In adults with spontaneous ICH, does admission to an organised stroke unit versus admission to a general ward reduce the risk of death or death/dependence?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: In adults with spontaneous ICH, we suggest limiting the use of outcome prediction scores to providing prognostic information, rather than using them as the primary or sole method for predicting outcomes for adults with ICH, given the risk of a self-fulfilling prophecy.

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 1: 1: Organised Stroke Unit Care In adults with spontaneous ICH, does admission to an organised stroke unit versus admission to a general ward reduce the risk of death or death/dependence?
allPracticeChanges.category: 1: Organised Stroke Unit Care In adults with spontaneous ICH
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In adults within 24 h of spontaneous ICH onset, there is insufficient evidence from randomised trials regarding the influence of policies on limitation of treatment and do-not-resuscitate orders on death and dependency.
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: 1: Organised Stroke Unit Care In adults with spontaneous ICH, does admission to an organised stroke unit versus admission to a general ward reduce the risk of death or death/dependence?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: In adults within 24 h of spontaneous ICH onset, we suggest not implementing general policies that limit treatment or initiate do not attempt cardiopulmonary resuscitation orders.

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 2: Acute Blood Pressure Alteration In adults with acute spontaneous ICH, does altering blood pressure (BP) to a lower target compared with either no use of BP alteration to a specific target or using targets different from the lower range, result in reduced death or dependence, death or haematoma expansion (HE)?
allPracticeChanges.category: Acute Blood Pressure Alteration In adults with acute spontan
allPracticeChanges.currentText: For adults with acute spontaneous ICH and systolic blood pressure of 150–220 mmHg, the overall balance of beneficial and adverse effects is uncertain, so we recommend recruitment to ongoing randomised controlled trials.
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: Acute Blood Pressure Alteration In adults with acute spontaneous ICH, does altering blood pressure (BP) to a lower target compared with either no use of BP alteration to a specific target or using targets different from the lower range, result in reduced death or dependence, death or haematoma expansion (HE)?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement:
1. We suggest lowering systolic blood pressure below 140 mmHg within 6 h of symptom onset in minor or moderate ICH (haematoma volume < 30 mL) to reduce haematoma expansion. 
2. For adults with spontaneous ICH, we suggest avoiding a reduction in systolic blood pressure of more than 70 mmHg from baseline and to avoid active reduction of systolic blood pressure below 110 mmHg. Caution is advised when lowering very high systolic blood pressure (>220 mmHg), for patients with large haematoma volumes (>30 mL) or when there is planned haematoma evacuation. 
3. For adults with spontaneous minor or moderate ICH (haematoma volume < 30 mL), we suggest applying the following aspects: 
- Initiating antihypertensive treatment as early as possible, ideally within the first 2 h following the onset of symptoms (acute phase): Lower systolic blood pressure to <140 mmHg and minimise variability in blood pressure fluctuations. 
- After lowering systolic blood pressure below the target threshold (up to 7 days, sub-acute phase): Maintain systolic blood pressure below 140 mmHg.
- For secondary prevention (after sub-acute phase): Follow the recommendations on secondary prevention, specifically section 6.1 on blood pressure management.

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 3: 1.1: Recombinant Factor VIIa (rFVIIa) for Non-Antithrombotic ICH In adults with spontaneous ICH not associated with antithrombotic drug use, does haemostatic therapy using rFVIIa versus placebo or open control reduce death or dependence, death or haematoma expansion and not increase thromboembolic adverse events?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: For adults with spontaneous ICH not associated with antithrombotic drug use, there is uncertainty about the balance of beneficial and adverse effects of rFVIIa, so we suggest against its routine use and suggest recruitment to ongoing randomised controlled trials.

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For adults with spontaneous ICH not associated with antithrombotic drug use, there is uncertainty about the balance of clinical benefits (functional outcome, death and dependence) and adverse effects of tranexamic acid. allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: 1.1: Recombinant Factor VIIa (rFVIIa) for Non-Antithrombotic ICH In adults with spontaneous ICH not associated with antithrombotic drug use, does haemostatic therapy using rFVIIa versus placebo or open control reduce death or dependence, death or haematoma expansion and not increase thromboembolic adverse events?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: Tranexamic acid may be considered for reducing haematoma expansion, if enrolment in an ongoing randomised controlled trial is not possible.

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In adults with ICH associated with use of vitamin K-antagonists (VKA), there is continuing uncertainty about the beneficial and adverse effects of PCC versus FFP on clinical outcomes.

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 3: 1.1: Recombinant Factor VIIa (rFVIIa) for Non-Antithrombotic ICH In adults with spontaneous ICH not associated with antithrombotic drug use, does haemostatic therapy using rFVIIa versus placebo or open control reduce death or dependence, death or haematoma expansion and not increase thromboembolic adverse events?

Given differences in results and quality of evidence for surgical interventions, recommendations are further specified for craniotomy (PICO 4.1.2), minimally invasive surgical removal (PICO 4.1.3), and surgery with catheter placement plus thrombolysis (PICO 4.1.4).

allPracticeChanges.category: 1.1: Physical Measures to Prevent Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT)
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In immobile adults with spontaneous ICH, we suggest for intermittent pneumatic compression stockings for 30 days (or hospital discharge or independent ambulation, if sooner) to prevent proximal deep vein thrombosis. Continued uncertainty exists whether intermittent pneumatic compression reduces symptomatic pulmonary embolism and death.

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In adults with spontaneous ICH, there is uncertainty whether subcutaneous low-molecular-weight heparins (LMWH) at prophylactic doses starting as early as 24 h after ICH onset and established stability of the ICH prevent venous thromboembolism, symptomatic deep vein thrombosis (DVT), pulmonary embolism (PE), or death, without increasing the risk of recurrent ICH, so we recommend recruitment to randomised controlled trials.

allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: Low-molecular-weight heparins (LMWH) prophylaxis after ICH might be used for venous thromboembolism prevention in standard clinical practice if intermittent pneumatic compression is not available or feasible. The use should be limited to immobile patients, as well as patients at high prothrombotic risk (due to comorbidities, or prothrombotic medications).

allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement:
1. We recommend implementing the components of the care bundle influencing our recommendation, which were: 
- Early intensive blood pressure management: with the goal of achieving a target systolic blood pressure of less than 140mmHg in minor to moderate ICH within 1h of the initiation of treatment (see also PICO 2 for details
- Control of elevated blood glucose: (target 110–141mg/dL (6.1–7.8mmol/L) without diabetes/141–180mg/dL (7.8–10mmol/L) with diabetes; avoiding hypoglycaemia) as soon as possible after the initiation of treatment 
- Treatment of pyrexia (target < 37.5°C within 1 h)
- Reversal of abnormal anticoagulation in VKA (target INR < 1.3 within 1 h) and DOACs. 
2. Additional components: avoiding DNR orders within first 24 h; routine dysphagia screening/treatment; early neurosurgical consultation.

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In adults with prior ICH, we recommend blood pressure control to reduce the risk of subsequent stroke. No evidence-based, specific recommendation can be made targeting a specific blood pressure level or choice of antihypertensive drug.

allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: We suggest blood pressure control to a target value of ≤130/80 mmHg in patients surviving ICH as a means to reduce the risk of subsequent stroke.

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In adults with spontaneous ICH and non-valvular atrial fibrillation (NVAF), there is uncertainty about the net benefit of long-term oral anticoagulation (OAC) to reduce the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events and death or dependence compared with the avoidance of OAC, so we encourage recruitment to randomised controlled trials.
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: 1: Secondary Prevention — Blood Pressure Control In adults with spontaneous ICH, does blood pressure reduction to a lower target, or with a specific agent, compared with standard care, or no specific agent or a higher target, reduce the risk of subsequent stroke, major vascular events, death, or dependence in patients in the post-acute phase?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: Direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) treatment after ICH in patients with non-valvular atrial fibrillation (NVAF) seems to increase the risk of recurrent ICH, but reduces the overall risk of major adverse cardiovascular events, so DOAC may be considered after careful evaluation of the individual risk-benefit profile.

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In adults with a history of prior ICH and non-valvular atrial fibrillation (NVAF), there is uncertainty about the effects of left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO) compared to long-term anticoagulation for the prevention of thromboembolic events, and we encourage enrolment in randomised controlled trials.
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: 1: Secondary Prevention — Blood Pressure Control In adults with spontaneous ICH, does blood pressure reduction to a lower target, or with a specific agent, compared with standard care, or no specific agent or a higher target, reduce the risk of subsequent stroke, major vascular events, death, or dependence in patients in the post-acute phase?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement:
1. Left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO) may be considered as a means to reduce thromboembolic events in adults with prior ICH and non-valvular atrial fibrillation (NVAF), who are considered unsuitable for long-term OAC therapy (e.g. people with imaging or pathological evidence of cerebral amyloid angiopathy), and we encourage enrolment of these patients in randomised controlled trials.
2. We suggest periprocedural antithrombotic treatment according to the recommendation provided by the European Society of Cardiology.

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In adults with spontaneous ICH who were taking antiplatelet therapy before the event, we suggest restarting antiplatelet therapy for a licensed indication is safe, but overall effects are uncertain.

allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: We suggest to consider restarting or initiating antiplatelet treatment if there is a licensed indication, ideally within randomised controlled trials. Antiplatelet therapy without a licensed indication should not be initiated outside of randomised controlled trials.

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In adults with a history of ICH, continuing uncertainty exists regarding secondary prevention with statin compared to no statin therapy to reduce recurrent ICH, major vascular events, or death. We recommend inclusion of suitable patients in ongoing randomised controlled trials.
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: 1: Secondary Prevention — Blood Pressure Control In adults with spontaneous ICH, does blood pressure reduction to a lower target, or with a specific agent, compared with standard care, or no specific agent or a higher target, reduce the risk of subsequent stroke, major vascular events, death, or dependence in patients in the post-acute phase?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: In adults with a history of ICH and an indication for statin use, we suggest initiating statin treatment over no use of statin therapy in patients with high cardiovascular risk in primary as well a secondary prevention after evaluation of the individual risk-benefit profile.

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For clinical practice, we suggest considering adding extra time of repetitive upper limb practice to existing stroke rehabilitation programmes. The exact amount of additional practice time is unclear but will likely be at least 20 h, commonly delivered 3–5 times per week over 4–6 weeks.

allPracticeChanges.category: In people with stroke, does adding at least 20 h or more of
allPracticeChanges.currentText: Due to the limited evidence of only a single RCT, we cannot make an overall recommendation that a certain amount of additional time spent in walking practice will have an additional effect on walking capacity in people with stroke.
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In people with stroke, does adding at least 20 h or more of same type of gait training produce greater improvements in walking independence, walking speed, walking endurance and walking capacity?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: Based on the overall available evidence, 13 out of 17 MWG members (76%) suggest that additional time spent in walking practice can improve walking capacity in people with stroke. The exact amount of the additional practice time is unclear but will likely be at least 20 h, commonly delivered 3–5 times per week over 4–6 weeks. Thus, for clinical practice, we suggest considering adding extra time of walking practice to existing stroke rehabilitation programmes, preferably at least 20 h.

allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In people with stroke, does high-intensity walking training compared to dose-matched (in duration) walking training at a lower intensity produce greater improvements in walking independence, walking speed, walking endurance and walking capacity?

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Due to the limited evidence, based only on a single RCT, we cannot make an overall recommendation that including a transfer package in upper limb therapy compared to not including a transfer package has an additional effect on upper limb activity capacity or performance.

allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: Acknowledging the current lack of evidence for this PICO, 13 out of 17 MWG members (76%) suggest considering a transfer package when providing repetitive upper limb task-specific training, when aiming to achieve a transfer from treatment to daily life. The transfer package would include daily evaluation, a patient-kept daily diary, problem-solving, behavioural contract, home practice of specified exercises, and weekly follow-up contacts.

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For clinical practice, we suggest task-specific group-based therapy being at least as effective as individual therapy for improving balance capacity, gait speed and walking endurance. A reasonable ratio between patients and therapists is required to ensure safety and supervision as well as offering additional individualised therapy  to address patients’ goals and preferences.

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For clinical practice, we suggest additional sit-to-stand practice on top of usual care to improve postural balance capacity. Additional training should include sufficient repetitions, training sessions and adequate duration and content of training. What these parameters are is currently unclear.

guidelines.title: 2025 ESO guideline on visual impairment in stroke
guidelines.executiveSummary: Evidence-based European clinical practice guideline dedicated to post-stroke visual dysfunction, standardizing screening for homonymous visual field deficits, spatial neglect, ocular motility disorders, and central visual processing deficits, recommending compensatory visual scanning training and optical prisms.

allPracticeChanges.topic: Compensatory Visual Scanning Training (VST) for Hemianopia and Visual Neglect
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In stroke patients with homonymous visual field defects or unilateral spatial neglect, we recommend structured compensatory visual scanning training (VST) consisting of systematic saccadic explorations to the blind hemifield to improve functional mobility, reading ability, and daily visual independence.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: Strong recommendation FOR, Moderate quality evidence
allPracticeChanges.previousText: Visual scanning exercises were considered an optional adjunct.
drivingTrials: Cochrane Interventions for Visual Field Defects 2024

allPracticeChanges.topic: Routine Multimodal Visual Screening Within 72 Hours of Stroke Admission
allPracticeChanges.currentText: We recommend that all hospitalized acute stroke patients undergo standardized screening for visual field loss, spatial neglect, and eye movement abnormalities within 72 hours of admission using validated bedside instruments (e.g., confrontation, line bisection, ocular alignment testing).
allPracticeChanges.previousText: Formal ophthalmic and orthoptic evaluations were ordered only upon patient complaint.

allPracticeChanges.topic: Fresnel Optical Prisms for Functional Visual Field Expansion
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In motivated stroke patients with dense homonymous hemianopia, we suggest the selective fitting of temporary Fresnel sector or monocular peli prisms on spectacle lenses to assist in detecting obstacles in the blind hemifield during ambulatory activities.
allPracticeChanges.previousText: Prisms were rarely prescribed due to reports of visual confusion.

allPracticeChanges.topic: Occlusion Strategies and Orthoptic Exercises for Post-Stroke Diplopia
allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients experiencing disabling diplopia due to stroke-induced cranial nerve (III, IV, VI) palsies or internuclear ophthalmoplegia, we suggest temporary monocular occlusion (foil/bangerter filter rather than opaque patch) or ground prisms combined with orthoptic convergence exercises.
allPracticeChanges.previousText: Complete eye patches were applied haphazardly without binocular re-evaluation.

allPracticeChanges.topic: Non-Invasive Brain Stimulation (rTMS / tDCS) for Unilateral Spatial Neglect
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In stroke patients with persisting unilateral spatial neglect unresponsive to conventional scanning, we suggest inhibitory low-frequency rTMS or cathodal tDCS over the unaffected left posterior parietal cortex, or excitatory anodal tDCS over the right parietal cortex, paired with active visual exploration therapy.
allPracticeChanges.previousText: Brain stimulation protocols were considered experimental.

allPracticeChanges.topic: High-Contrast Digital Typographical Aids for Hemianopic Alexia
allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients experiencing hemianopic reading difficulties (hemianopic alexia), we suggest structured optokinetic reading training software and digital high-contrast reading aids to expand text reading speed and comprehension.
allPracticeChanges.previousText: Patients were provided standard non-customized magnifying glasses.
drivingTrials: Digital Reading Adaptation in Hemianopia Cohorts

guidelines.title: 2023 AHA ASA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage
topTakeaways: 1. [7. Surgical - Class 3: Harm, Level B-NR] For patients with aSAH from ruptured saccular aneurysms amenable to either primary coiling or clipping, stents or flow diverters should not be used to avoid higher risk of complications.
2. [8. Management of Medical Complications - Class 3: Harm, Level B-R] In patients with aSAH, induction of hypervolemia is potentially harmful because of the association with excess morbidity.
3. [8.3 Management of Vasospasm - Class 3: Harm, Level B-R] For patients with aSAH at risk of DCI, prophylactic hemodynamic augmentation should not be performed to reduce iatrogenic patient harm.
4. [8.5 Management of Seizures - Class 3: Harm, Level B-NR] In patients with aSAH, phenytoin for seizure prevention and/or antiseizure prophylaxis is associated with excess morbidity and mortality.

5. [3. Natural History - Class 3: No Benefit, Level B-NR] In patients with aSAH who do not improve after correction of modifiable conditions and are deemed unsalvageable because of evidence of irreversible neurological injury, treatment of the aneurysm is not beneficial.
6. [6. Medical Measures to Prevent Rebleeding - Class 3: No Benefit, Level A] In patients with aSAH, routine use of antifibrinolytic therapy is not useful to improve functional outcome.
7. [7.1 Anesthetic Management - Class 3: No Benefit, Level B-R] In patients with good-grade aSAH, the routine use of induced mild hypothermia during aneurysm surgery is not beneficial.
8. [8.3 Management of Vasospasm - Class 3: No Benefit, Level A] In patients with aSAH, routine use of statin therapy to improve outcomes is not recommended.
9. [8.3 Management of Vasospasm - Class 3: No Benefit, Level A] In patients with aSAH, routine use of intravenous magnesium to improve neurological outcomes is not recommended.

10. [8.4 Management of Hydrocephalus - Class 3: No Benefit, Level C-LD] In patients with aSAH, routine fenestration of the lamina terminalis is not indicated for reducing the rate of shunt dependency.
guidelines.executiveSummary: Hướng dẫn thực hành lâm sàng chính thức từ AHA/ASA. Bao gồm 84 khuyến cáo then chốt được trích xuất và kiểm chứng qua hệ thống AI Lõi NeuroGuide.

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with aSAH, use of clinical scales (eg, the Hunt and Hess [HH] grade or World Federation of Neurosurgical Societies [WFNS] grade) is recommended to determine initial clinical severity and predict outcome.
In patients with high-grade aSAH, aneurysm treatment is reasonable, after careful discussion of likely prognosis with family members, to optimize patient outcome.
drivingTrials: Meta-Analysis by Zhao et al. 2017 (85 studies

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with aSAH and advanced age, aneurysm treatment is reasonable, after careful discussion of prognosis with family members, to improve survival and outcome.
drivingTrials: Barrow Ruptured Aneurysm Trial (BRAT) Substudy (Catapano et al. 2021)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with aSAH who do not improve after correction of modifiable conditions and are deemed unsalvageable because of evidence of irreversible neurological injury, treatment of the aneurysm is not beneficial.
In patients with acute onset of severe headache, prompt diagnostic workup and evaluation are recommended to diagnose/exclude aSAH and minimize morbidity and mortality.

In patients with acute onset of severe headache who present >6 hours from symptom onset or who have a new neurological deficit, a noncontrast head CT and, if negative for aSAH, lumbar puncture (LP) should be performed to diagnose/exclude aSAH.

In patients with acute onset of severe headache who present <6 hours from symptom onset and without new neurological deficit, a noncontrast head CT performed on a high-quality scanner and interpreted by a board-certified neuroradiologist is reasonable to diagnose/exclude aSAH.
drivingTrials: Meta-Analysis by Dubosh et al. 2016 (8907 patients

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with acute onset of severe headache without a new neurological deficit, application of the Ottawa SAH Rule may be reasonable to identify those at high risk for aSAH.

In patients with spontaneous SAH with high level of concern for aneurysmal source and a negative or inconclusive CT angiography (CTA), digital subtraction angiography (DSA) is indicated to diagnose/exclude cerebral aneurysm(s).
In patients with SAH from confirmed cerebral aneurysm(s), DSA can be useful to determine the optimal strategy for aneurysm intervention.

For patients with aSAH, timely transfer from hospitals with low case volume to higher-volume centers with multidisciplinary neurointensive care services, comprehensive stroke center capabilities, and experienced cerebrovascular surgeons/neuroendovascular interventionalists is recommended to improve outcomes.
For patients with aSAH, care should be provided in a dedicated neurocritical care unit by a multidisciplinary team.
drivingTrials: PRINCE Study Part 1 & 2 (Venkatasubba Rao et al. 2020

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with aSAH and unsecured aneurysm, frequent blood pressure (BP) monitoring and BP control with short-acting medication(s) is recommended to avoid severe hypotension, hypertension, and BP variability.
In patients with aSAH who are receiving anticoagulants, emergency anticoagulation reversal with appropriate reversal agents should be performed to prevent rebleeding.
drivingTrials: NCS/SCCM Antithrombotic Reversal Guideline (Frontera et al. 2016)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with aSAH, routine use of antifibrinolytic therapy is not useful to improve functional outcome.
drivingTrials: ULTRA Landmark RCT (Post et al. Lancet 2021)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with aSAH, surgical or endovascular treatment of the ruptured aneurysm should be performed as early as feasible after presentation, preferably within 24 hours of onset, to improve outcome.
For patients with aSAH, complete obliteration of the ruptured aneurysm is indicated whenever feasible to reduce the risk of rebleeding and retreatment.

For patients with aSAH in whom complete obliteration of the ruptured aneurysm by either clipping or primary coiling treatment is not feasible in the acute phase, partial obliteration to secure the rupture site and retreatment in a delayed fashion in those with functional recovery are reasonable to prevent rebleeding.
For patients with aSAH from ruptured aneurysms of the posterior circulation that are amenable to coiling, coiling is indicated in preference to clipping to improve outcome.
For patients with aSAH deemed salvageable and with depressed level of consciousness due to large intraparenchymal hematoma, emergency clot evacuation should be performed to reduce mortality.
drivingTrials: Heiskanen et al. 1988 (RCT showing 27% vs 80% mortality benefit)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with aSAH, the ruptured aneurysm should be evaluated by specialist(s) with endovascular and surgical expertise to determine the relative risks and benefits of surgical or endovascular treatment according to patient and aneurysm characteristics.
For patients >70 years of age with aSAH, the superiority of coiling or clipping to improve outcome is not well established.
drivingTrials: ISAT Trial Subgroup Analysis (Molyneux et al. 2005

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients <40 years of age with aSAH, clipping of the ruptured aneurysm might be considered the preferred mode of treatment to improve durability of the treatment and outcome.
drivingTrials: ISAT Trial Subgroup Analysis (Molyneux et al. 2005

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with good-grade aSAH from ruptured aneurysms of the anterior circulation equally suitable for both primary coiling and clipping, primary coiling is recommended in preference to clipping to improve 1-year functional outcome.
drivingTrials: ISAT Landmark RCT (Molyneux et al. Lancet 2002

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with good-grade aSAH from ruptured aneurysms of the anterior circulation equally suitable for both primary coiling and clipping, both treatment options are reasonable to achieve favorable long-term outcome.
drivingTrials: ISAT Long-Term Follow-up (van Donkelaar et al. 2020

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with aSAH from ruptured wide-neck aneurysms not amenable to surgical clipping or primary coiling, endovascular treatment with stent-assisted coiling or flow diverters is reasonable to reduce the risk of rebleed.
For patients with aSAH from ruptured fusiform/blister aneurysms, the use of flow diverters is reasonable to reduce mortality.
For patients with aSAH from ruptured saccular aneurysms amenable to either primary coiling or clipping, stents or flow diverters should not be used to avoid higher risk of complications.
In patients with aSAH, the intraoperative use of mannitol or hypertonic saline can be effective in reducing ICP and cerebral edema.
In patients with aSAH, anesthetic goals should include minimizing postprocedural pain, nausea, and vomiting.
In patients with aSAH, prevention of intraoperative hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia during aneurysm surgery is reasonable to improve outcomes.
In patients with aSAH and an unsecured ruptured aneurysm, frequent intraoperative BP monitoring and BP control are reasonable to prevent ischemia and rerupture.
In patients with aSAH, intraoperative neuromonitoring may be reasonable to guide anesthetic and operative management.

In patients with aSAH and an uncontrolled intraoperative aneurysmal rupture, adenosine may be considered to facilitate aneurysm clip placement by inducing cardiac standstill and temporary profound pause.
In patients with good-grade aSAH, the routine use of induced mild hypothermia during aneurysm surgery is not beneficial.
drivingTrials: IHAST Landmark RCT (Todd et al. NEJM 2005

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with aSAH who require mechanical ventilation for >24 hours, implementation of a standardized ICU care bundle is recommended to reduce the duration of mechanical ventilation and hospital-acquired pneumonia.
drivingTrials: BI-VILI Quality Improvement Project (Asehnoune et al. Intensive Care Med 2017)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with aSAH who develop severe acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and life-threatening hypoxemia, rescue maneuvers such as prone positioning and alveolar recruitment maneuvers with ICP monitoring may be reasonable to improve oxygenation.
In patients with aSAH, close monitoring and goal-directed treatment of volume status are reasonable to maintain euvolemia.
In patients with aSAH, use of mineralocorticoids is reasonable to treat natriuresis and hyponatremia.
In patients with aSAH, induction of hypervolemia is potentially harmful because of the association with excess morbidity.
In patients with aSAH whose ruptured aneurysm has been secured, pharmacological or mechanical venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis is recommended to reduce the risk for VTE.
drivingTrials: CLOTS 3 Landmark RCT (Dennis et al. Lancet 2013

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with aSAH, effective glycemic control, strict hyperglycemia management, and avoidance of hypoglycemia are reasonable to improve outcome.
In patients with aSAH with fever refractory to antipyretic medications, the effectiveness of therapeutic temperature management (TTM) during the acute phase of aSAH is uncertain.
drivingTrials: PAIS Trial (den Hertog et al. Lancet Neurol 2009)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with aSAH, use of evidence-based protocols and order sets is recommended to improve standardization of care.
drivingTrials: QASC Cluster RCT (Middleton et al. Lancet 2011

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with aSAH, frequent neurological assessment with a neurological assessment tool such as the GCS or National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) is recommended to monitor DCI and other secondary complications.
drivingTrials: VASOGRADE Scale (de Oliveira Manoel et al. Stroke 2015)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with aSAH, frequent vital sign and neurological monitoring is recommended for detection of neurological change and prevention of secondary cerebral insults and poor outcomes.
In patients with aSAH, a validated dysphagia screening protocol should be implemented before initiation of oral intake to reduce the incidence of pneumonia.
In patients with aSAH, specialized nursing stroke competencies and certification can be effective to positively affect outcomes, timeliness of care, and adherence to stroke protocols.
In patients with aSAH and a secured aneurysm, an early, evidence-based mobility algorithm is reasonable to improve level of function at discharge and global functional outcome at 12 months.
In patients with aSAH with suspected vasospasm or limited neurological examination, CTA or CT perfusion (CTP) can be useful to detect vasospasm and predict DCI.
In patients with aSAH, transcranial Doppler (TCD) ultrasound monitoring is reasonable to detect vasospasm and predict DCI.
In patients with high-grade aSAH, continuous EEG (cEEG) monitoring can be useful to predict DCI.
In patients with high-grade aSAH, invasive monitoring of brain tissue oxygenation, lactate/pyruvate ratio, and glutamate may be considered to predict DCI.
In patients with aSAH, early initiation of enteral nimodipine is beneficial in preventing DCI and improving functional outcomes.
drivingTrials: Allen et al. Landmark NEJM Trial 1983

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with aSAH, maintaining euvolemia can be beneficial in preventing DCI and improving functional outcomes.
In patients with aSAH and symptomatic vasospasm, elevating systolic BP values may be reasonable to reduce the progression and severity of DCI.
In patients with aSAH and severe vasospasm, use of intra-arterial vasodilator therapy may be reasonable to reverse cerebral vasospasm and reduce the progression and severity of DCI.
In patients with aSAH and severe vasospasm, cerebral angioplasty may be reasonable to reverse cerebral vasospasm and reduce the progression and severity of DCI.
drivingTrials: BPAV Phase II RCT (Zwienenberg-Lee et al. 2008)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with aSAH, routine use of statin therapy to improve outcomes is not recommended.
drivingTrials: Meta-Analyses by Shen et al. 2017 & Vergouwen et al. 2010 (6 RCTs
no significant benefit in DCI or mortality)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with aSAH, routine use of intravenous magnesium to improve neurological outcomes is not recommended.
drivingTrials: IMASH Phase III RCT (Wong et al. Stroke 2010)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with aSAH at risk of DCI, prophylactic hemodynamic augmentation should not be performed to reduce iatrogenic patient harm.
In patients with aSAH and acute symptomatic hydrocephalus, urgent CSF diversion (EVD and/or lumbar drainage) should be performed to improve neurological outcome.

In patients with aSAH and hydrocephalus who require an EVD, implementation and adherence to an EVD bundled protocol that addresses insertion, management, education, and monitoring are recommended to reduce complication and infection rates.
In patients with aSAH and associated chronic symptomatic hydrocephalus, permanent CSF diversion is recommended to improve neurological outcome.
In patients with aSAH, routine fenestration of the lamina terminalis is not indicated for reducing the rate of shunt dependency.
drivingTrials: Meta-Analysis by Komotar et al. 2009 (11 studies

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with aSAH and either fluctuating neurological examination, depressed mental state, ruptured MCA aneurysm, high-grade SAH, ICH, hydrocephalus, or cortical infarction, cEEG monitoring is reasonable to detect seizures.

In patients with aSAH and high-seizure-risk features (ie, ruptured MCA aneurysm, high-grade SAH, ICH, hydrocephalus, and cortical infarction), use of prophylactic antiseizure medication(s) may be reasonable to prevent seizures.

In patients with aSAH without high-seizure-risk features (ie, ruptured MCA aneurysm, high-grade SAH, ICH, hydrocephalus, and cortical infarction), prophylactic treatment with antiseizure medication is not beneficial.
In patients with aSAH, phenytoin for seizure prevention and/or antiseizure prophylaxis is associated with excess morbidity and mortality.
In patients with aSAH who present with seizures, treatment with antiseizure medications for ≤7 days is reasonable to reduce seizure-related complications in the perioperative period.
In patients with aSAH without prior epilepsy who present with seizures, treatment with antiseizure medications beyond 7 days is not effective for reducing future SAH-associated seizure risk.
In patients with aSAH, use of validated grading scores or patient-reported outcome measures prior to hospital discharge is recommended to screen for physical, cognitive, behavioral, and QOL deficits.
In patients with aSAH, use of validated screening tools in the postacute period is recommended to identify post-aSAH depression and anxiety.
In patients with aSAH and depression, psychotherapy and pharmacotherapy are recommended to reduce symptoms of depression.
drivingTrials: Legg et al. Cochrane SSRI Review 2019 (RR 0.75)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with aSAH, use of a validated screening tool in the postacute period is useful to identify cognitive dysfunction.
In patients with aSAH, an early multidisciplinary team–based approach to treatment and rehabilitation is recommended to reduce LOS and identify discharge needs.
drivingTrials: Alaraj et al. 2017 (LOS reduced from 21.6 to 14.1 days)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with aSAH and no other medical or neurological contraindications, early rehabilitation after the ruptured aneurysm is secured is reasonable to improve functional outcome and reduce LOS.
In patients with aSAH in a coma, early use of neurostimulants may be reasonable to promote consciousness recovery.
In patients with aSAH without depression, fluoxetine therapy is not effective to enhance poststroke functional status.
In adult patients with aSAH, screening and intervention for depression, anxiety, and sexual dysfunction are recommended to improve long-term outcomes.
drivingTrials: von Vogelsang et al. EQ-5D 10-Yr Study 2013

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with aSAH, it is reasonable to choose the MoCA over the MMSE to identify cognitive impairment.
In patients with aSAH, counseling patients and caregivers on the high long-term risk of cognitive dysfunction can be beneficial to identify long-term needs.
drivingTrials: Corraini et al. 30-Year Cohort Study 2017 (HR for dementia 2.72)

allPracticeChanges.topic: 10. Risk Factors & Monitoring for Recurrent aSAH
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with aSAH who have undergone aneurysm repair, perioperative cerebrovascular imaging is recommended to identify remnants or recurrence of the aneurysm that may require further treatment.

allPracticeChanges.topic: 10. Risk Factors & Monitoring for Recurrent aSAH
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with aSAH who have undergone aneurysm repair, follow-up cerebrovascular imaging is recommended to identify recurrence or regrowth of the treated aneurysm, changes in another known aneurysm, or development of de novo aneurysm(s) that may require further treatment to reduce the risk of aSAH.
