guidelines.title: 2022 AHA/ASA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Spontaneous Intracerebral Hemorrhage
guidelines.executiveSummary: Complete Synoptic Table of Verbatim Recommendations, Class of Recommendation (COR), Level of Evidence (LOE), and Key Referenced Studies

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with stroke, including spontaneous ICH, design and implementation of stroke public education programs for diverse populations focused on early recognition and the need to seek emergency care rapidly is useful to reduce time to diagnosis and treatment.

In patients with sudden onset of neurological symptoms or signs attributable to potential spontaneous ICH, use of stroke recognition and severity tools is recommended for dispatch personnel and first responders to identify potential stroke and facilitate rapid transport to reduce time to diagnosis and treatment.

In patients with stroke symptoms attributable to potential spontaneous ICH, immediate activation of the emergency response system (9-1-1 in North America) is recommended to reduce time to diagnosis and treatment.
drivingTrials: Ekundayo et al. Get With The Guidelines-Stroke 2013

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with potential spontaneous ICH, early notification by emergency medical services (EMS) staff to the receiving hospital is recommended to improve time to diagnosis and treatment.

In patients with spontaneous ICH, regional systems of stroke care are recommended so all potentially beneficial therapies can be made available when appropriate as rapidly as possible, including, at minimum, (a) health care facilities that provide initial spontaneous ICH care, including diagnosis and treatment, and (b) health care facilities with neurocritical care and neurosurgical capabilities.

In patients with potential stroke, including spontaneous ICH, in geographic regions where mobile stroke units (MSUs) operate, such mobile units are reasonable to enable more rapid diagnosis and treatment than achievable by ambulance transfer to the closest stroke-capable facility.

In patients with potential spontaneous ICH, first responder training in stroke evaluation and care with the ability to provide airway and circulatory support when necessary is reasonable to detect and manage prehospital neurological deterioration (ND).

In patients with spontaneous ICH, focused history, physical examination, and routine laboratory work and tests on hospital admission (eg, complete blood count, prothrombin time/international normalized ratio [INR]/partial thromboplastin time, creatinine/estimated glomerular filtration rate, glucose, cardiac troponin and ECG, toxicology screen, and inflammatory markers) should be performed to help identify the type of hemorrhage, active medical issues, and risk of unfavorable outcomes.
In patients presenting with stroke-like symptoms, rapid neuroimaging with CT or MRI is recommended to confirm the diagnosis of spontaneous ICH.
In patients with spontaneous ICH and/or IVH, serial head CT can be useful within the first 24 hours after symptom onset to evaluate for hemorrhage expansion.

In patients with spontaneous ICH and/or IVH and with low GCS score or ND, serial head CT can be useful to evaluate for hemorrhage expansion, development of hydrocephalus, brain swelling, or herniation.
In patients with spontaneous ICH, CT angiography (CTA) within the first few hours of ICH onset may be reasonable to identify patients at risk for subsequent HE.
drivingTrials: PREDICT Study (Demchuk et al. Lancet Neurol 2012)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with spontaneous ICH, using noncontrast computed tomography (NCCT) markers of HE to identify patients at risk for HE may be reasonable.

In patients with lobar spontaneous ICH and age <70 years, deep/posterior fossa spontaneous ICH and age <45 years, or deep/posterior fossa and age 45 to 70 years without history of hypertension, acute CTA plus consideration of venography is recommended to exclude macrovascular causes or cerebral venous thrombosis.
drivingTrials: DIAGRAM Study Group (van Asch et al. BMJ 2015

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with spontaneous IVH and no detectable parenchymal hemorrhage, catheter intra-arterial digital subtraction angiography (DSA) is recommended to exclude a macrovascular cause.

In patients with spontaneous ICH and a CTA or magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) suggestive of a macrovascular cause, catheter intra-arterial DSA should be performed as soon as possible to confirm and manage underlying intracranial vascular malformations.
drivingTrials: Delgado Almandoz et al. sICH Score 2010

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with (a) lobar spontaneous ICH and age <70 years, (b) deep/posterior fossa ICH and age <45 years, or (c) deep/posterior fossa and age 45 to 70 years without history of hypertension and negative noninvasive imaging (CTA±venography and MRI/MRA), catheter intra-arterial DSA is reasonable to exclude a macrovascular cause.

In patients with spontaneous ICH with a negative CTA/venography, it is reasonable to perform MRI and MRA to establish a nonmacrovascular cause of ICH (such as CAA, deep perforating vasculopathy, cavernous malformation, or malignancy).

In patients with spontaneous ICH who undergo CT or MRI at admission, CTA plus consideration of venography or MRA plus consideration of venography performed acutely can be useful to exclude macrovascular causes or cerebral venous thrombosis.

In patients with spontaneous ICH and a negative catheter intra-arterial DSA and no clear microvascular diagnosis or other defined structural lesion, it may be reasonable to perform a repeat catheter intra-arterial DSA 3 to 6 months after ICH onset to identify a previously obscured vascular lesion.

In patients with spontaneous ICH requiring acute BP lowering, careful titration to ensure continuous smooth and sustained control of BP, avoiding peaks and large variability in SBP, can be beneficial for improving functional outcomes.
drivingTrials: Moullaali et al. INTERACT2/ATACH-2 IPD Meta-Analysis 2019

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with spontaneous ICH in whom acute BP lowering is considered, initiating treatment within 2 hours of ICH onset and reaching target within 1 hour can be beneficial to reduce the risk of HE and improve functional outcome.

In patients with spontaneous ICH of mild to moderate severity presenting with SBP between 150 and 220 mm Hg, acute lowering of SBP to a target of 140 mm Hg with the goal of maintaining in the range of 130 to 150 mm Hg is safe and may be reasonable for improving functional outcomes.
In patients with spontaneous ICH presenting with large or severe ICH or those requiring surgical decompression, the safety and efficacy of intensive BP lowering are not well established.
drivingTrials: Qureshi et al. ATACH-2 Post Hoc 2020

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with spontaneous ICH of mild to moderate severity presenting with SBP >150 mm Hg, acute lowering of SBP to <130 mm Hg is potentially harmful.

In patients with anticoagulant-associated spontaneous ICH, anticoagulation should be discontinued immediately and rapid reversal of anticoagulation should be performed as soon as possible after diagnosis of spontaneous ICH to improve survival.

In patients with VKA-associated spontaneous ICH and INR ≥2.0, 4-factor (4-F) prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) is recommended in preference to fresh-frozen plasma (FFP) to achieve rapid correction of INR and limit HE.
drivingTrials: INCH Landmark RCT (Steiner et al. Lancet Neurol 2016)
Sarode et al. Phase IIIb RCT 2013

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with VKA-associated spontaneous ICH, intravenous vitamin K should be administered directly after coagulation factor replacement (PCC or other) to prevent later increase in INR and subsequent HE.
In patients with VKA-associated spontaneous ICH with INR of 1.3 to 1.9, it may be reasonable to use PCC to achieve rapid correction of INR and limit HE.
In patients with direct factor Xa inhibitor–associated spontaneous ICH, andexanet alfa is reasonable to reverse the anticoagulant effect of factor Xa inhibitors.
In patients with dabigatran-associated spontaneous ICH, idarucizumab is reasonable to reverse the anticoagulant effect of dabigatran.
drivingTrials: RE-VERSE AD Trial (Pollack et al. NEJM 2017)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with direct factor Xa inhibitor–associated spontaneous ICH, a 4-F PCC or activated PCC (aPCC) may be considered to improve hemostasis.

In patients with dabigatran- or factor Xa inhibitor–associated spontaneous ICH, when the DOAC agent was taken within the previous few hours, activated charcoal may be reasonable to prevent absorption of the DOAC.
drivingTrials: Ollier et al. 2017; van Ryn et al. 2009

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with dabigatran-associated spontaneous ICH, when idarucizumab is not available, aPCC or PCCs may be considered to improve hemostasis.
In patients with dabigatran-associated spontaneous ICH, when idarucizumab is not available, renal replacement therapy (RRT) may be considered to reduce dabigatran concentration.
In patients with unfractionated heparin (UFH)–associated spontaneous ICH, intravenous protamine is reasonable to reverse the anticoagulant effect of heparin.
In patients with low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH)–associated spontaneous ICH, intravenous protamine may be considered to partially reverse the anticoagulant effect of heparin.
drivingTrials: Schulman & Bijsterveld 2007; van Veen et al. 2011

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with spontaneous ICH being treated with aspirin and who require emergency neurosurgery, platelet transfusion might be considered to reduce postoperative bleeding and mortality.
For patients with spontaneous ICH being treated with antiplatelet agents, the effectiveness of desmopressin with or without platelet transfusions to reduce the expansion of the hematoma is uncertain.
For patients with spontaneous ICH being treated with aspirin and not scheduled for emergency surgery, platelet transfusions are potentially harmful and should not be administered.
drivingTrials: PATCH Landmark Phase III RCT (Baharoglu et al. Lancet 2016)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with spontaneous ICH (with or without the spot sign), the effectiveness of recombinant factor VIIa to improve functional outcome is unclear.
drivingTrials: FAST Phase III RCT (Mayer et al. NEJM 2008
SPOTLIGHT & STOP-IT RCTs (Gladstone et al. JAMA Neurol 2019)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with spontaneous ICH (with or without the spot sign, black hole sign, or blend sign), the effectiveness of TXA to improve functional outcome is not well established.
drivingTrials: TICH-2 Landmark Phase III RCT (Sprigg et al. Lancet 2018)
STOP-AUST RCT (Meretoja et al. Lancet Neurol 2020)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with spontaneous ICH, provision of care in a specialized inpatient (eg, stroke) unit with a multidisciplinary team is recommended to improve outcomes and reduce mortality.
drivingTrials: Stroke Unit Trialists' Collaboration Meta-Analyses (Langhorne et al. Stroke 2013

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with spontaneous ICH, provision of care at centers that can provide the full range of high-acuity care and expertise is recommended to improve outcomes.

In patients with spontaneous ICH and clinical hydrocephalus, transfer to centers with neurosurgical capabilities for definitive hydrocephalus management (eg, EVD placement and monitoring) is recommended to reduce mortality.
In patients with spontaneous ICH, care delivery that includes multidisciplinary teams trained in neurological assessment is recommended to improve outcomes.

In hospitalized patients with spontaneous ICH who require hospital transfer but do not have adequate airway protection, cannot support adequate gas exchange, and/or do not have a stable hemodynamic profile, appropriate life-sustaining therapies should be initiated before transportation to prevent acute medical decompensation in transport.
drivingTrials: Consensus Guidance / Standard Critical Care Practice

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with spontaneous ICH without indications for ICU admission at presentation, initial provision of care in a stroke unit compared with a general ward is reasonable to reduce mortality and improve outcomes.

In patients with moderate to severe spontaneous ICH, IVH, hydrocephalus, or infratentorial location, provision of care in a neuro-specific ICU compared with a general ICU is reasonable to improve outcomes and reduce mortality.
In patients with IVH or infratentorial ICH location, transfer to centers with neurosurgical capabilities might be reasonable to improve outcomes.
In patients with larger supratentorial ICH, transfer to centers with neurosurgical capabilities may be reasonable to improve outcomes.
In patients with spontaneous ICH, the use of standardized protocols and/or order sets is recommended to reduce disability and mortality.
In patients with spontaneous ICH, a formal dysphagia screening protocol should be implemented before initiation of oral intake to reduce disability and the risk of pneumonia.
In patients with spontaneous ICH, continuous cardiac monitoring for the first 24 to 72 hours of admission is reasonable to monitor for cardiac arrhythmias and new cardiac ischemia.
In patients with spontaneous ICH, diagnostic laboratory and radiographic testing for infection on admission and throughout the hospital course is reasonable to improve outcomes.
In nonambulatory patients with spontaneous ICH, intermittent pneumatic compression (IPC) starting on the day of diagnosis is recommended for VTE (DVT and pulmonary embolism [PE]) prophylaxis.
drivingTrials: CLOTS 3 Landmark RCT (Dennis et al. Lancet 2013)
Yogendrakumar et al. Systematic Review & Network Meta-Analysis 2020

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In nonambulatory patients with spontaneous ICH, low-dose UFH or LMWH can be useful to reduce the risk for PE.

In nonambulatory patients with spontaneous ICH, initiating low-dose UFH or LMWH prophylaxis at 24 to 48 hours from ICH onset may be reasonable to optimize the benefits of preventing thrombosis relative to the risk of HE.
In nonambulatory patients with spontaneous ICH, graduated compression stockings of knee-high or thigh-high length alone are not beneficial for VTE prophylaxis.
drivingTrials: CLOTS 1 & 2 Landmark RCTs (Dennis et al. Lancet 2009

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with acute spontaneous ICH and proximal DVT who are not yet candidates for anticoagulation, the temporary use of a retrievable filter is reasonable as a bridge until anticoagulation can be initiated.
For patients with acute spontaneous ICH and proximal DVT or PE, delaying treatment with UFH or LMWH for 1 to 2 weeks after the onset of ICH might be considered.

In patients with spontaneous ICH, frequent neurological assessments (including GCS) should be performed by ED nurses in the early hyperacute phase of care to assess change in status, neurological examination, or level of consciousness.
In patients with spontaneous ICH, frequent neurological assessments in the ICU and stroke unit are reasonable for up to 72 hours of admission to detect early ND.
In patients with spontaneous ICH, specialized nurse stroke competencies can be effective in improving outcome and mortality.
In patients with spontaneous ICH, monitoring serum glucose is recommended to reduce the risk of hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia.
In patients with spontaneous ICH, treating hypoglycemia (<40–60 mg/dL, <2.2–3.3 mmol/L) is recommended to reduce mortality.
drivingTrials: Oddo et al. 2008; van den Berghe et al. NEJM 2001

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with spontaneous ICH, treating moderate to severe hyperglycemia (>180–200 mg/dL, >10.0–11.1 mmol/L) is reasonable to improve outcomes.
In patients with spontaneous ICH, pharmacologically treating an elevated temperature may be reasonable to improve functional outcomes.
drivingTrials: PAIS Phase III RCT (den Hertog et al. Lancet Neurol 2009)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with spontaneous ICH, the usefulness of therapeutic hypothermia (<35° C/95 °F) to decrease peri-ICH edema is unclear.
In patients with spontaneous ICH, impaired consciousness, and confirmed electrographic seizures, antiseizure drugs should be administered to reduce morbidity.
drivingTrials: Mehta et al. Nationwide Inpatient Sample 2018

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with spontaneous ICH and clinical seizures, antiseizure drugs are recommended to improve functional outcomes and prevent brain injury from prolonged recurrent seizures.
drivingTrials: ILAE Consensus Guidelines & Clinical Practice Standards

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with spontaneous ICH and unexplained abnormal or fluctuating mental status or suspicion of seizures, continuous electroencephalography (≥24 hours) is reasonable to diagnose electrographic seizures and epileptiform discharges.
In patients with spontaneous ICH without evidence of seizures, prophylactic antiseizure medication is not beneficial to improve functional outcomes, long-term seizure control, or mortality.
In patients with spontaneous ICH or IVH and hydrocephalus that is contributing to decreased level of consciousness, ventricular drainage should be performed to reduce mortality.
In patients with moderate to severe spontaneous ICH or IVH with a reduced level of consciousness, ICP monitoring and treatment might be considered to reduce mortality and improve outcomes.
In patients with spontaneous ICH, the efficacy of early prophylactic hyperosmolar therapy for improving outcomes is not well established.
In patients with spontaneous ICH, bolus hyperosmolar therapy may be considered for transiently reducing ICP.
In patients with spontaneous ICH, corticosteroids should not be administered for treatment of elevated ICP.

For patients with supratentorial ICH of >20- to 30-mL volume with GCS scores in the moderate range (5–12), minimally invasive hematoma evacuation with endoscopic or stereotactic aspiration with or without thrombolytic use can be useful to reduce mortality compared with medical management alone.
drivingTrials: MISTIE III Landmark Phase III RCT (Hanley et al. Lancet 2019

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with supratentorial ICH of >20- to 30-mL volume with GCS scores in the moderate range (5–12) being considered for hematoma evacuation, it may be reasonable to select minimally invasive hematoma evacuation over conventional craniotomy to improve functional outcomes.

For patients with supratentorial ICH of >20- to 30-mL volume with GCS scores in the moderate range (5–12), the effectiveness of minimally invasive hematoma evacuation with endoscopic or stereotactic aspiration with or without thrombolytic use to improve functional outcomes is uncertain.
drivingTrials: MISTIE III Phase III RCT (Hanley et al. 2019)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with spontaneous ICH, large IVH, and impaired level of consciousness, EVD is recommended in preference to medical management alone to reduce mortality.

For patients with a GCS score >3 and primary IVH or IVH extension from spontaneous supratentorial ICH of <30-mL volume requiring EVD, minimally invasive IVH evacuation with EVD plus thrombolytic is safe and is reasonable compared with EVD alone to reduce mortality.
drivingTrials: CLEAR III Landmark Phase III RCT (Hanley et al. Lancet 2017)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with a GCS score >3 and primary IVH or IVH extension from spontaneous supratentorial ICH of <30-mL volume requiring EVD, the effectiveness of minimally invasive IVH evacuation with EVD plus thrombolytic use to improve functional outcomes is uncertain.
drivingTrials: CLEAR III Phase III RCT (Hanley et al. 2017)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with severe spontaneous ICH, large IVH, and impaired level of consciousness, the efficacy of EVD for improving functional outcomes is not well established.

For patients with spontaneous supratentorial ICH of <30-mL volume and IVH requiring EVD, the usefulness of minimally invasive IVH evacuation with neuroendoscopy plus EVD, with or without thrombolytic, to improve functional outcomes and reduce permanent shunt dependence is uncertain.
For most patients with spontaneous supratentorial ICH of moderate or greater severity, the usefulness of craniotomy for hemorrhage evacuation to improve functional outcomes or mortality is uncertain.
drivingTrials: STICH I Landmark RCT (Mendelow et al. Lancet 2005)
STICH II Landmark RCT (Mendelow et al. Lancet 2013)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with supratentorial ICH who are deteriorating, craniotomy for hematoma evacuation might be considered as a lifesaving measure.

For patients with cerebellar ICH who are deteriorating neurologically, have brainstem compression and/or hydrocephalus from ventricular obstruction, or have cerebellar ICH volume ≥15 mL, immediate surgical removal of the hemorrhage with or without EVD is recommended in preference to medical management alone to reduce mortality.
drivingTrials: Kuramatsu et al. Propensity-Matched IPD Meta-Analysis (JAMA 2019)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with supratentorial ICH who are in a coma, have large hematomas with significant midline shift, or have elevated ICP refractory to medical management, decompressive craniectomy with or without hematoma evacuation may be considered to reduce mortality.

In patients with supratentorial ICH who are in a coma, have large hematomas with significant midline shift, or have elevated ICP refractory to medical management, effectiveness of decompressive craniectomy with or without hematoma evacuation to improve functional outcomes is uncertain.
In patients with spontaneous ICH, administering a baseline measure of overall hemorrhage severity is recommended as part of the initial evaluation to provide an overall measure of clinical severity.
drivingTrials: Gregório et al. Systematic Reviews & Meta-Analyses 2018

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with spontaneous ICH, a baseline severity score might be reasonable to provide a general framework for communication with the patient and their caregivers.
In patients with spontaneous ICH, a baseline severity score should not be used as the sole basis for forecasting individual prognosis or limiting life-sustaining treatment.

In patients with spontaneous ICH who do not have preexisting documented requests for life-sustaining therapy limitations, aggressive care, including postponement of new DNAR orders or withdrawal of medical support until at least the second full day of hospitalization, is reasonable to decrease mortality and improve functional outcome.

In patients with spontaneous ICH who are unable to fully participate in medical decision-making, use of a shared decision-making model between surrogates and physicians is reasonable to optimize the alignment of care with patient wishes and surrogate satisfaction.

In patients with spontaneous ICH who have DNAR status, limiting other medical and surgical interventions, unless explicitly specified by the patient or surrogate, is associated with increased patient mortality.

In patients with spontaneous ICH, multidisciplinary rehabilitation, including regular team meetings and discharge planning, should be performed to improve functional outcome and reduce morbidity and mortality.
drivingTrials: Stroke Unit Trialists' Collaboration Meta-Analyses (Langhorne et al. Stroke 2013

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with spontaneous ICH with mild to moderate severity, early supported discharge is beneficial to increase the likelihood of patients living at home at 3 months.
drivingTrials: Early Supported Discharge Trialists (Langhorne et al. Cochrane 2017)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with spontaneous ICH with moderate severity, early rehabilitation beginning 24 to 48 hours after onset (including ADL training, stretching, functional task training) may be considered to improve functional outcome and reduce mortality.
drivingTrials: HeadPoST Cluster RCT (Anderson et al. NEJM 2017)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with spontaneous ICH without depression, fluoxetine therapy is not effective to enhance poststroke functional status.
In patients with spontaneous ICH, very early and intense mobilization within the first 24 hours is associated with lower likelihood of good recovery.
drivingTrials: AVERT Landmark Phase III RCT (Avert Trial Collaboration Lancet 2015)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with spontaneous ICH and moderate to severe depression, appropriate evidence-based treatments including psychotherapy and pharmacotherapy are useful to reduce symptoms of depression.
In patients with spontaneous ICH, administration of depression and anxiety screening tools in the postacute period is recommended to identify patients with poststroke depression and anxiety.
In patients with spontaneous ICH, administration of a cognitive screening tool in the postacute period is useful to identify patients with cognitive impairment and dementia.
In patients with spontaneous ICH and cognitive impairment, referral for cognitive therapy is reasonable to improve cognitive outcomes.
In patients with spontaneous ICH and pre-existing or new mood disorders requiring pharmacotherapy, continuation or initiation of SSRIs after ICH can be beneficial for the treatment of mood disorders.
In patients with spontaneous ICH and cognitive impairment, treatment with cholinesterase inhibitors or memantine might be considered to improve cognitive outcomes.

In patients with spontaneous ICH in whom the risk for recurrent ICH may facilitate prognostication or management decisions, it is reasonable to incorporate the following risk factors for ICH recurrence into decision-making: (a) lobar location of the initial ICH; (b) older age; (c) presence, number, and lobar location of microbleeds on MRI; (d) presence of disseminated cortical superficial siderosis on MRI; (e) poorly controlled hypertension; (f) Asian or Black race; and (g) presence of apolipoprotein E ε2 or ε4 alleles.
In patients with spontaneous ICH, BP control is recommended to prevent hemorrhage recurrence.
drivingTrials: PROGRESS Landmark RCT (Chapman et al. Stroke 2004

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with spontaneous ICH, it is reasonable to lower BP to an SBP of 130 mm Hg and diastolic BP (DBP) of 80 mm Hg for long-term management to prevent hemorrhage recurrence.
drivingTrials: PRoFESS Trial Subanalysis (Hilkens et al. Neurology 2017)
Biffi et al. JAMA 2015; 2017 ACC/AHA Hypertension Guidelines

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with spontaneous ICH and conditions placing them at high risk of thromboembolic events, for example, a mechanical valve or LVAD, early resumption of anticoagulation to prevent thromboembolic complications is reasonable.
drivingTrials: Kuramatsu et al. Eur Heart J 2018

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with spontaneous ICH with an indication for antiplatelet therapy, resumption of antiplatelet therapy may be reasonable for the prevention of thromboembolic events based on consideration of benefit and risk.
drivingTrials: RESTART Landmark Open-Label RCT (RESTART Collaboration Lancet 2019

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation (AF) and spontaneous ICH, the resumption of anticoagulation to prevent thromboembolic events and reduce all-cause mortality may be considered based on weighing benefit and risk.

In patients with AF and spontaneous ICH in whom the decision is made to restart anticoagulation, initiation of anticoagulation ≈7 to 8 weeks after ICH may be considered after weighing specific patient characteristics to optimize the balance of risks and benefits.
In patients with AF and spontaneous ICH deemed ineligible for anticoagulation, left atrial appendage closure may be considered to reduce the risk of thromboembolic events.
drivingTrials: PROTECT-AF & PREVAIL Landmark RCTs Meta-Analyses (Reddy et al. JACC 2017

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with spontaneous ICH and an established indication for statin pharmacotherapy, the risks and benefits of statin therapy on ICH outcomes and recurrence relative to overall prevention of cardiovascular events are uncertain.
In patients with spontaneous ICH, regular long-term use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) is potentially harmful because of the increased risk of ICH.
In patients with spontaneous ICH, lifestyle modification is reasonable to reduce BP.
drivingTrials: Multimodal Secondary Prevention Meta-Analyses (Wang et al. Br J Sports Med 2019)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with spontaneous ICH, avoiding heavy alcohol consumption is reasonable to reduce hypertension and risk of ICH recurrence.
drivingTrials: Alcohol & Stroke Risk Population Cohorts & Meta-Analyses

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with spontaneous ICH, lifestyle modification, including supervised training and counseling, may be reasonable to improve functional recovery.
In patients with spontaneous ICH, psychosocial education for the caregiver can be beneficial to increase patients’ activity level and participation and/or quality of life.
In patients with spontaneous ICH, practical support and training for the caregiver are reasonable to improve patients’ standing balance.

When considering primary prevention of ICH, it may be reasonable to incorporate any available MRI results demonstrating cerebral microbleed burden or cortical superficial siderosis to inform shared decision-making about stroke prevention treatment plans.
drivingTrials: CROMIS-2 Study (Wilson et al. Lancet Neurol 2018

guidelines.executiveSummaryVi: Hướng dẫn thực hành lâm sàng chính thức từ AHA/ASA (2022) về Xuất huyết não tự phát (ICH), tổng hợp hệ thống 124 khuyến cáo phân tầng mức độ chỉ định (COR) và mức độ bằng chứng (LOE) cùng dữ liệu từ các thử nghiệm lâm sàng đối chứng then chốt.

guidelines.title: 2026 ESO EANS and ESMINT guideline on aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage
guidelines.executiveSummary: Hướng dẫn thực hành lâm sàng chính thức từ ESO. Bao gồm 17 khuyến cáo đã được bác sĩ chuyên khoa phê duyệt.

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 1a In adult patients with aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage (aSAH), does treatment with antifibrinolytic drugs compared to no antifibrinolytic drugs decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In adult patients with aSAH, we recommend against routine administration of antifibrinolytic drugs prior to treatment of the ruptured aneurysm to decrease the risk of poor functional outcome.
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In adult patients with aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage (aSAH), does treatment with antifibrinolytic drugs compared to no antifibrinolytic drugs decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 1b In adult patients with aSAH, does treatment with antihypertensive drugs compared to no antihypertensive drugs decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In adult patients with aSAH, no recommendation can be made on the administration of blood pressure lowering drugs prior to treatment of the ruptured aneurysm to decrease the risk of poor functional outcome.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Uncertain / Ongoing trials (Evidence: Very low, Voting: Vote: 11/13)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In adult patients with aSAH, does treatment with antihypertensive drugs compared to no antihypertensive drugs decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement:
1. In adult patients with aSAH and systolic blood pressures higher than 160-180 mm Hg persisting after installment of analgesics, oral nimodipine and urinary catheter prior to aneurysm treatment, we suggest considering blood pressure lowering drugs to lower systolic blood pressure to around 160 mm Hg to reduce the risk of rebleeding. (Vote: 11/13)
2. If it is decided to give blood pressure lowering drugs, we suggest continuous infusion of short-acting drugs, e.g. labetalol, and avoiding diuretic drugs to maintain normovolemia. Care should be taken to ensure that the blood pressure reduction is gradual, with systolic blood pressure reduced cautiously over time (corresponding to no more than a 10% reduction in mean arterial pressure within the first 2 hours) to decrease the risk of DCI. (Vote: 11/13)

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 2 In adult patients with aSAH, does early aneurysm occlusion compared to no early aneurysm occlusion decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In adult patients with aSAH, no recommendation can be made on treating the ruptured aneurysm as early as possible to decrease the risk of poor functional outcome.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Uncertain / Ongoing trials (Evidence: Very low, Voting: Vote: 13/13)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In adult patients with aSAH, does early aneurysm occlusion compared to no early aneurysm occlusion decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: In adult patients with aSAH, we suggest treatment of the ruptured aneurysm within 24 hours after ictus. The timing should be optimized to ensure that the most dedicated team of experts is available when needed. (Vote: 13/13)

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 3a In adult patients with aSAH, does any type of endovascular aneurysm occlusion compared to neurosurgical aneurysm occlusion decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In adult patients with aSAH in good clinical condition (WFNS I-III) with aneurysms of either the anterior or posterior circulation that can be treated by either regular coiling (i.e. without adjunctive devices) or neurosurgical clipping, we recommend regular coiling as the preferred strategy to decrease the risk of poor functional outcome.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Strong for intervention (Evidence: High, Voting: Vote: 13/13)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In adult patients with aSAH, does any type of endovascular aneurysm occlusion compared to neurosurgical aneurysm occlusion decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement:
1. We suggest that all patients with aSAH are discussed in an interdisciplinary manner, with at least one neurosurgeon and one neuro-interventionalist. (Vote: 13/13)
2. In adult patients with aSAH, we suggest that the team discuss which modality would result in the best clinical outcome of the specific patient, with the safest and optimal occlusion of the specific aneurysm. (Vote: 13/13)
3. In adult patients with aSAH younger than 45 years of age, we suggest that the better long-term protection from clipping compared to coiling is taken into consideration for choosing the treatment modality of the aneurysm. (Vote: 12/13)
4. In adult patients with aSAH admitted in a poor clinical condition (defined as GCS < 13), we suggest a multidisciplinary approach to decide on type and timing of aneurysm treatment taking into account the (presumed) cause of the poor clinical condition. (Vote: 13/13)
5. In adult patients with aSAH and a poor or worsening clinical condition from a space-occupying intracerebral or subdural haematoma, we suggest immediate surgery for aneurysm clipping and haematoma removal. (Vote: 11/13)

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 3b In adult patients with aSAH, does any type of endovascular aneurysm treatment other than coiling compared to coiling of the ruptured aneurysm decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In adult patients with aSAH, no recommendation can be made on the use of endovascular treatment options other than regular coiling for treatment of the ruptured aneurysm to decrease the risk of poor functional outcome.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Uncertain / Ongoing trials (Evidence: Very low, Voting: Vote: 13/13)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In adult patients with aSAH, does any type of endovascular aneurysm treatment other than coiling compared to coiling of the ruptured aneurysm decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement:
1. Given the limited comparative evidence available, we suggest that in adult patients with subarachnoid haemorrhage from a ruptured aneurysm which cannot be treated with regular coiling, the multidisciplinary team discusses the safety, effectiveness, and durability of microsurgical and alternative endovascular options to determine the preferred treatment strategy. (Vote: 12/13)
2. In adult patients with aSAH, we suggest stent-assisted coiling in selected cases where other treatment options are not feasible. (Vote: 13/13)
3. In adult patients with aSAH, we suggest to reserve flow diversion as a last-line treatment option. (Vote: 12/13)

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 4 In adult patients with aSAH, does any type of medical treatment aiming to reduce the risk of delayed cerebral ischaemia (DCI) compared to no such treatment decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In adult patients with aSAH, we recommend prophylactic treatment with oral nimodipine to decrease the risk of poor functional outcome.
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In adult patients with aSAH, does any type of medical treatment aiming to reduce the risk of delayed cerebral ischaemia (DCI) compared to no such treatment decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 4 In adult patients with aSAH, does any type of medical treatment aiming to reduce the risk of delayed cerebral ischaemia (DCI) compared to no such treatment decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In adult patients with aSAH, we do not recommend prophylactic treatment with either tirilazad, statins, magnesium sulfate, or endothelin receptor antagonists to decrease the risk of poor functional outcome.
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In adult patients with aSAH, does any type of medical treatment aiming to reduce the risk of delayed cerebral ischaemia (DCI) compared to no such treatment decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 4 In adult patients with aSAH, does any type of medical treatment aiming to reduce the risk of delayed cerebral ischaemia (DCI) compared to no such treatment decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In adult patients with aSAH, no recommendation can be made on prophylactic treatment with antiplatelet drugs or lumbar drainage to decrease the risk of poor functional outcome until further data from RCT are available.
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In adult patients with aSAH, does any type of medical treatment aiming to reduce the risk of delayed cerebral ischaemia (DCI) compared to no such treatment decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 5a In adult patients with aSAH and clinical deterioration due to delayed cerebral ischaemia, does hypertension induction compared to no hypertension induction decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In adult patients with aSAH and clinical deterioration due to delayed cerebral ischaemia, no recommendation can be made on hypertension induction to decrease the risk of poor functional outcome.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Uncertain / Ongoing trials (Evidence: Low, Voting: Vote: 11/13)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In adult patients with aSAH and clinical deterioration due to delayed cerebral ischaemia, does hypertension induction compared to no hypertension induction decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: In adult patients with aSAH and clinical deterioration due to delayed cerebral ischaemia, we suggest considering induced hypertension, provided that the ruptured aneurysm is treated and after standard therapy has proven insufficient. Clinical contraindications and potential complications of induced hypertension should be considered. (Vote: 11/13)

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 5b In adult patients with aSAH and clinical deterioration due to delayed cerebral ischaemia, does endovascular treatment of vasospasm compared to no endovascular treatment decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In adult patients with aSAH and clinical deterioration due to delayed cerebral ischaemia, no recommendation can be made on endovascular treatment of vasospasm to decrease the risk of poor functional outcome.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Uncertain / Ongoing trials (Evidence: Low, Voting: Vote: 13/13)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In adult patients with aSAH and clinical deterioration due to delayed cerebral ischaemia, does endovascular treatment of vasospasm compared to no endovascular treatment decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement:
1. In adult patients with aSAH and clinical deterioration due to delayed cerebral ischaemia in combination with refractory and severe vasospasm, we suggest considering intra-arterial pharmacological treatment as a rescue therapy in selected patients to decrease the risk of poor functional outcome. (Vote: 11/13)
2. In adult patients with aSAH and clinical deterioration due to delayed cerebral ischaemia in combination with refractory severe vasospasm, the current evidence is insufficient to support the routine use of mechanical vasodilatation with balloon angioplasty. In selected cases, this approach may be considered as a last-line rescue treatment after careful multidisciplinary discussion of the potential risks and uncertain benefits. (Vote: 12/13)
3. In adult patients with aSAH and clinical deterioration due to delayed cerebral ischaemia in combination with refractory severe vasospasm, the current data are insufficient to support the use of mechanical vasodilatation with temporary deployment of retrievable stents to decrease the risk of poor functional outcome. (Vote: 13/13)

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 6a In adult patients with aSAH, does any type of neuroimaging compared to regular neurological examination decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In adult patients with aSAH, no recommendation can be made on neuroimaging to decrease the risk of poor functional outcome.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Uncertain / Ongoing trials (Evidence: Very low, Voting: Vote: 13/13)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In adult patients with aSAH, does any type of neuroimaging compared to regular neurological examination decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement:
1. In adult patients with aSAH and clinical deterioration, we suggest plain head CT in combination with CT-Perfusion (CTP) imaging to detect the cause of deterioration. (Vote: 11/13)
2. In adult patients with aSAH who are neurologically not assessable but at high risk for DCI, we suggest plain head CT and CTP at least once between day 4 and 14. (Vote: 10/13)
3. In adult patients with aSAH, we do not suggest a routine DSA for screening of macrovascular vasospasm. (Vote: 13/13)

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 6b In adult patients with aSAH, does any type of neuromonitoring compared to regular neurological examination decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In adult patients with aSAH, no recommendation can be made on neuromonitoring to decrease the risk of poor functional outcome.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Uncertain / Ongoing trials (Evidence: Very low, Voting: Vote: 13/13)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In adult patients with aSAH, does any type of neuromonitoring compared to regular neurological examination decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement:
1. In adult patients with aSAH, no suggestion can be given on the use of TCD monitoring. (Vote: 10/13)
2. In adult patients with aSAH and radiological hydrocephalus who are neurologically not assessable, we suggest ICP monitoring via EVD if an EVD is in place. (Vote: 13/13)
3. In adult patients with aSAH without radiological hydrocephalus who are neurologically not assessable, no suggestion can be given on ICP monitoring. (Vote: 11/13)
4. In adult patients with aSAH who are neurologically not assessable, we do not suggest invasive multimodal neuromonitoring with continuous measurement of partial pressure of brain tissue oxygen (PbtO2) and/or microdialysis due to the uncertain risk/benefit ratio of these modalities. (Vote: 10/13)
5. In adult patients with aSAH who are neurologically not assessable, we do not suggest the routine use of continuous EEG monitoring. (Vote: 13/13)

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 7 In adult patients with aSAH, does treatment of hydrocephalus (either by EVD, VP-shunt or lumbar drainage) compared to no treatment of hydrocephalus decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In adult patients with aSAH and hydrocephalus, no recommendation can be made on CSF diversion strategies to decrease the risk of poor functional outcome.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Uncertain / Ongoing trials (Evidence: Very low, Voting: Vote: 13/13)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In adult patients with aSAH, does treatment of hydrocephalus (either by EVD, VP-shunt or lumbar drainage) compared to no treatment of hydrocephalus decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement:
1. In adult patients with aSAH who present with radiological hydrocephalus and a decreased level of consciousness, we suggest CSF drainage. (Vote: 13/13)
2. In adult patients with aSAH who present with obstructive hydrocephalus and a decreased level of consciousness, we suggest EVD placement. (Vote: 13/13)
3. In adult patients with aSAH who present with communicating hydrocephalus and a decreased level of consciousness, we suggest LD or repeated LPs as the strategy of first choice for CSF drainage. (Vote: 11/13)
4. In adult patients with aSAH who present with radiological hydrocephalus and a normal level of consciousness, we do not suggest CSF drainage. (Vote: 12/13)
5. In adult patients with aSAH who come at a point at which prolonged CSF drainage (by EVD, LD or repeated LPs) carries a higher risk of severe complications than placement of a permanent CSF diversion, we suggest permanent CSF diversion. (Vote: 13/13)
6. In adult patients with aSAH who present with symptomatic chronic hydrocephalus, we suggest permanent CSF diversion. (Vote: 13/13)

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 8 In adult patients with aSAH, does treatment on a dedicated neuro-ICU or high care unit compared to a general ICU or high care unit decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In adult patients with aSAH, no recommendation can be made on admission to a dedicated neuro-ICU or high care unit to decrease the risk of poor functional outcome.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Uncertain / Ongoing trials (Evidence: Very low, Voting: Vote: 13/13)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In adult patients with aSAH, does treatment on a dedicated neuro-ICU or high care unit compared to a general ICU or high care unit decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: In adult patients with aSAH, we suggest admission and management in a dedicated neuro-ICU or high care unit to decrease the risk of poor functional outcome. (Vote: 13/13)

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 9a In adult patients with aSAH, does treatment in a high-volume centre compared to a low-volume centre decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In adult patients with aSAH, no recommendation can be made on admission/transfer to a high-volume centre to decrease the risk of poor functional outcome.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Uncertain / Ongoing trials (Evidence: Very low, Voting: Vote: 12/13)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In adult patients with aSAH, does treatment in a high-volume centre compared to a low-volume centre decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: We suggest that all patients with spontaneous SAH are admitted or immediately transferred to centres that treat at least 70 patients with aSAH per year, or at least 35 patients with aSAH per year in remote areas where access is limited. (Vote: 12/13)

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 9b In adult patients with aSAH, does aneurysm treatment by a high-volume neurosurgeon or neurointerventionalist compared to a low-volume neurosurgeon or neurointerventionalist decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In adult patients with aSAH, no recommendation can be made on case-volume per neurosurgeon and neurointerventionalist to decrease the risk of poor functional outcome.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Uncertain / Ongoing trials (Evidence: Very low, Voting: Vote: 12/13)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In adult patients with aSAH, does aneurysm treatment by a high-volume neurosurgeon or neurointerventionalist compared to a low-volume neurosurgeon or neurointerventionalist decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: In adult patients with aSAH, we suggest that aneurysms are repaired by neurosurgeons or neurointerventionalists who perform the treatment of choice in more than 30 patients with aneurysms (ruptured and unruptured) per year. (Vote: 12/13)

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 10 In adult patients with aSAH, does a radiological follow-up beyond 6 months after aneurysm treatment compared to a maximum radiological follow-up duration of 6 months decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In adult patients with aSAH, no recommendation can be made on radiological follow-up beyond 6 months after microsurgical or endovascular aneurysm treatment to decrease the risk of poor functional outcome.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Uncertain / Ongoing trials (Evidence: Very low, Voting: Vote: 13/13)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In adult patients with aSAH, does a radiological follow-up beyond 6 months after aneurysm treatment compared to a maximum radiological follow-up duration of 6 months decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement:
1. In adult patients with aSAH who are treated with coils and adequate occlusion within 6 months, we suggest at least one additional radiological follow-up at or beyond 12 months after aneurysm repair to investigate potential aneurysm recanalization, as long as a potential re-treatment remains an option. (Vote: 13/13)
2. In adult patients with aSAH who were treated with clip reconstruction and adequate occlusion within 6 months, we do not suggest further radiological follow-up to investigate potential aneurysm recanalization. (Vote: 11/13)
3. In adult patients with aSAH who have neck remnants or partially occluded aneurysms (irrespective of type of aneurysm treatment), we suggest radiological follow-up beyond 6 months after aneurysm treatment as long as a potential re-treatment remains an option. (Vote: 13/13)
4. In adult patients with aSAH who are treated with endovascular devices other than coils, we suggest radiological follow-up at least five years after treatment, regardless of the degree of occlusion, to ensure adequate long-term occlusion and as long as a potential re-treatment remains an option. (Vote: 11/13)
5. In adult patients with aSAH, we suggest radiological follow-up beyond 6 months after aneurysm treatment in order to evaluate for de novo aneurysms at 5-year intervals as long as a potential treatment remains an option, in those with a high-risk profile (such as young age, positive family history for aSAH, autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease). (Vote: 12/13)

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 1: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset, does use of any standardised diagnostic criteria for SAP, compared to non-standardised clinician-based diagnosis, improve clinical outcomes?
allPracticeChanges.category: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset, there are insufficient data to support recommendations on whether the use of standardised diagnostic criteria for SAP improves clinical outcomes. Consequently, no evidence-based recommendation can be made. Please see the Expert Consensus Statement below.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Uncertain / Ongoing trials (Evidence: Uncertain / Ongoing trial, Voting: Vote: 8/8)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset, does use of any standardised diagnostic criteria for SAP, compared to non-standardised clinician-based diagnosis, improve clinical outcomes?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: In the absence of appropriately designed RCTs, and on the basis of observational studies and secondary analysis of RCTs, we suggest to use an algorithm-based approach for SAP diagnosis (for example PISCES) guided by a minimum set of agreed criteria. This may improve diagnostic accuracy and require further evaluation in research in clinical practice.

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 2: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset, does use of chest ultrasound or computed tomography to diagnose SAP, compared to chest X-ray alone, increase diagnostic accuracy and improve clinical outcomes?
allPracticeChanges.category: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset, uncertainty remains regarding the most accurate diagnostic approach for SAP when using chest ultrasound or computed tomography compared with chest X-ray alone. The potential benefits and risks of these procedures in relation to clinical outcomes are also unclear. Therefore, no evidence-based recommendation can currently be made. Please see the Expert Consensus Statement below.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Uncertain / Ongoing trials (Evidence: Uncertain / Ongoing trial, Voting: Vote: 8/8)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset, does use of chest ultrasound or computed tomography to diagnose SAP, compared to chest X-ray alone, increase diagnostic accuracy and improve clinical outcomes?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: We suggest to consider a pulmonary CT scan if SAP is suspected and the diagnosis uncertain, particularly where there is a need to inform further antibiotic/ medical therapy and/or exclude other pathologies (e.g. pulmonary embolism).

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 3: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset, does incorporation of any diagnostic (blood) biomarker, compared to not making use of diagnostic (blood) biomarkers, increase diagnostic accuracy and improve clinical outcomes?
allPracticeChanges.category: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset, there is insufficient data to make an evidence-based recommendation and continued uncertainty of the role of blood inflammatory or stress biomarkers in the diagnostic approach to SAP. Please see the Expert Consensus Statement below.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Uncertain / Ongoing trials (Evidence: Uncertain / Ongoing trial, Voting: Vote: 8/8)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset, does incorporation of any diagnostic (blood) biomarker, compared to not making use of diagnostic (blood) biomarkers, increase diagnostic accuracy and improve clinical outcomes?
drivingTrials: MAPS Trial secondary analysis (Warusevitane et al.
STROKE-INF Trial secondary analysis (Kalra et al.
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: We suggest considering the addition of CRP to standardised diagnostic algorithms for SAP to improve diagnostic accuracy in afebrile patients, with available data indicating cut-off values between 30 and 40 mg/L. (Voting: 8/8)

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 4: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset, does use of clinical prediction scores or biomarkers, compared to not using clinical prediction scores or biomarkers, identify patients who will develop SAP?
allPracticeChanges.category: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset, clinical prediction scores and selected biomarkers may help identify individuals at increased risk of developing SAP, with moderate to good discriminatory performance. However, there is currently insufficient evidence to support the routine combination of biomarkers with existing clinical prediction tools for risk stratification. Continued uncertainty remains regarding the incremental clinical value of these approaches, and their implementation will ultimately depend on the availability, feasibility, and effectiveness of targeted preventive interventions. Please refer to the Expert Consensus Statement below.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Weak for intervention (Evidence: Very low, Voting: Vote: 8/8)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset, does use of clinical prediction scores or biomarkers, compared to not using clinical prediction scores or biomarkers, identify patients who will develop SAP?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: We suggest using validated clinical prediction scores or biomarkers to identify patients at increased risk of SAP and to better target preventive standard measures. However, their clinical utility is currently limited by only moderate to good discriminatory performance and is likely to depend on the availability of more effective preventive treatment strategies.

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 5: In hospitalised adults with stroke associated pneumonia (ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke; non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset, does antibiotic treatment guided by clinical prediction scores or biomarkers, compared to standard clinical practice, improve clinical outcomes?
allPracticeChanges.category: In hospitalised adults with stroke associated pneumonia (isc
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset, there are currently insufficient data to support an evidence-based recommendation regarding the routine use of clinical prediction scores or blood biomarkers to guide antibiotic treatment of SAP. Please see the Expert Consensus Statement below.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Uncertain / Ongoing trials (Evidence: Uncertain / Ongoing trial, Voting: Vote: 8/8)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In hospitalised adults with stroke associated pneumonia (ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke; non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset, does antibiotic treatment guided by clinical prediction scores or biomarkers, compared to standard clinical practice, improve clinical outcomes?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: Due to insufficient evidence, we advise against using clinical prediction scores or biomarkers to guide antibiotic treatment of SAP. For information on the start and duration of antibiotic therapy, the choice of antibiotic, and the role of microbiological tests, please refer to PICO questions 12 to 14. (Voting: 8/8)

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 6: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset, does preventive antibiotic treatment compared to no preventive antibiotic treatment reduce SAP frequency and improve clinical outcomes?
allPracticeChanges.category: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic
allPracticeChanges.currentText: Recommendation 1. In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset, we suggest not using preventive antibiotic therapy, as it has not been shown to reduce the incidence of SAP.

Please see the Expert Consensus Statement below.

drivingTrials: Statins: Rodriguez de Antonio et al. (2011)
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: Antiemetics: We suggest not to administer antiemetics for the prevention of SAP hospitalized, non-ventilated adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke within 7 days of symptom onset outside of clinical trials, as there is insufficient evidence for this indication. However, we suggest using these drugs for the treatment of nausea and vomiting, guided by local guidelines and clinical judgement. A large phase 3 randomised controlled trial investigating metoclopramide for preventing SAP in the first two weeks after stroke is currently ongoing.

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 7: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset, does usage of specific drugs (e.g. beta-blockers, statins, acid-suppressing medication) compared to no usage of these specific drugs affect SAP frequency and clinical outcomes?
allPracticeChanges.category: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic
allPracticeChanges.currentText: Beta-blockers: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset, there is no evidence from RCTs or observational studies to determine whether starting beta-blockers after stroke prevents pneumonia. We are therefore unable to make an evidence-based recommendation. Please see the Expert Consensus Statement below.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Uncertain / Ongoing trials (Evidence: Uncertain / Ongoing trial, Voting: Vote: 8/8)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset, does usage of specific drugs (e.g. beta-blockers, statins, acid-suppressing medication) compared to no usage of these specific drugs affect SAP frequency and clinical outcomes?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: Beta Blockers: In hospitalised, non-ventilated adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke within 7 days of symptom onset, we suggest not to initiate beta-blockers for the prevention of SAP. However, if patients are taking beta-blockers for other reasons after the stroke, these should be continued, as there is no reason to stop them and weak evidence for a reduction in mortality.

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 7: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset, does usage of specific drugs (e.g. beta-blockers, statins, acid-suppressing medication) compared to no usage of these specific drugs affect SAP frequency and clinical outcomes?

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Statins: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset, there is insufficient evidence to make an evidence-based recommendation regarding the use of statins for the prevention of pneumonia. Please see the Expert Consensus Statement below.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Uncertain / Ongoing trials (Evidence: Uncertain / Ongoing trial, Voting: Vote: 8/8)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset, does usage of specific drugs (e.g. beta-blockers, statins, acid-suppressing medication) compared to no usage of these specific drugs affect SAP frequency and clinical outcomes?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: Statins: In hospitalised, non-ventilated adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke within 7 days of symptom onset, we suggest not to initiate statins for the purpose of preventing SAP. Where statins have been started for other indications, they should be continued.

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 7: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset, does usage of specific drugs (e.g. beta-blockers, statins, acid-suppressing medication) compared to no usage of these specific drugs affect SAP frequency and clinical outcomes?
allPracticeChanges.category: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic
allPracticeChanges.currentText: Other preventive treatments: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset, there is insufficient evidence to recommend the use/avoidance of ACEIs/ARBs, antacids, PPIs and H2 RAs, and benzodiazepines for the prevention of stroke-associated pneumonia. Please see the Expert Consensus Statement below.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Uncertain / Ongoing trials (Evidence: Very low, Voting: Voting: 8/8)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset, does usage of specific drugs (e.g. beta-blockers, statins, acid-suppressing medication) compared to no usage of these specific drugs affect SAP frequency and clinical outcomes?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: Other preventive treatments: In hospitalised, non-ventilated adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke within 7 days of symptom onset, concomitant medications prescribed for other indications may influence the risk of SAP. Acid-suppressive therapy may increase SAP risk, whereas treatment with ACEIs or ARBs in patients with intracerebral haemorrhage may be associated with reduced pneumonia and mortality risk. Given the limited evidence, we suggest considering these potential effects and using these medications strictly according to their primary indications, i.e. PPIs/H2 antagonists for the prevention and treatment of peptic ulceration, and ACEIs or ARBs for the management of hypertension.

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 8: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset who require nasogastric feeding, does intermittent feeding via the nasogastric tube, compared to continuous feeding via the nasogastric tube, reduce SAP frequency and improve clinical outcomes?
allPracticeChanges.category: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset who require nasogastric feeding, there is continued uncertainty regarding the balance of benefits and risks of intermittent feeding compared with continuous enteral feed delivery. Please see the Expert Consensus Statement below.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Uncertain / Ongoing trials (Evidence: Uncertain / Ongoing trial, Voting: Vote: 8/8)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset who require nasogastric feeding, does intermittent feeding via the nasogastric tube, compared to continuous feeding via the nasogastric tube, reduce SAP frequency and improve clinical outcomes?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: Given the limited evidence for intermittent versus continuous nasogastric feeding, with no clear evidence favoring either approach, we suggest to use the feeding mode with which clinicians and their teams are most familiar. (Voting: 8/8)

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 9: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset, do physical treatments to improve lung function, compared to no physical treatments to improve lung function, reduce SAP frequency and improve clinical outcomes?
allPracticeChanges.category: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset, there is currently insufficient evidence to support an evidence-based recommendation regarding the use of physical treatments to improve lung function for the prevention of SAP or improvement of outcome. Please see the Expert Consensus Statement below.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Uncertain / Ongoing trials (Evidence: Uncertain / Ongoing trial, Voting: Vote: 8/8)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset, do physical treatments to improve lung function, compared to no physical treatments to improve lung function, reduce SAP frequency and improve clinical outcomes?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: In hospitalised, non-ventilated adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke within 7 days of symptom onset, we suggest respiratory physiotherapy as part of an early post-stroke rehabilitation programme to prevent SAP. This is based on evidence suggesting improvements in respiratory function and reductions in respiratory complications when delivered over several weeks—primarily during the rehabilitation phase and often in combination with other interventions—as well as a trend towards reduced SAP and mortality in a meta-analysis of two small studies. (Voting: 8/8)

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 10: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset, do early physical treatments to address mobility, compared to no early physical treatments to address mobility, reduce SAP frequency and improve clinical outcomes?
allPracticeChanges.category: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset, we suggest that physical interventions to promote mobilization, either within bed or out of bed, should be initiated early (within 48 hours) to prevent SAP. Please see the Expert Consensus Statement below.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Weak for intervention (Evidence: Very low, Voting: Vote: 8/8)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset, do early physical treatments to address mobility, compared to no early physical treatments to address mobility, reduce SAP frequency and improve clinical outcomes?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: In hospitalised, non-ventilated adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke within 7 days of symptom onset, we therefore suggest to mobilise within the 48 hour window for the prevention of SAP. However, based on the results of the AVERT study very early (within less than 24 h of onset) and prolonged mobilisation out of bed should be avoided in patients with severe strokes, as it is associated with worse outcomes in that group. (Voting: 8/8)

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 11: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset who have reduced level of consciousness, does positioning in the recovery position, compared to no specific positioning, reduce SAP frequency and improve clinical outcomes?
allPracticeChanges.category: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset and a reduced level of consciousness, there is currently no clinical trial evidence to support recommendations on the use of the recovery position for preventing SAP. Please refer to the expert consensus statement below.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Uncertain / Ongoing trials (Evidence: Uncertain / Ongoing trial, Voting: Vote: 8/8)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset who have reduced level of consciousness, does positioning in the recovery position, compared to no specific positioning, reduce SAP frequency and improve clinical outcomes?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: Based on the results of a single small study (turn-mob) we suggest that patients, including those with reduced level of consciousness, should be turned from supine to the left and right lateral recumbent position every 2 hours during the day and mobilized passively in bed to prevent SAP, if they are unable to change position independently. In line with clinical practice and guidance for enteral feeding, we suggest that during and after enteral feeds patients should be nursed in the 30-45 degree head-up position to avoid aspiration. Guided by the results of the HeadPost study, we suggest that alert patients with mild strokes and without enteral tubes in place should maintain any position they find comfortable.

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 12: In hospitalised adults with stroke associated pneumonia (ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke; non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset, does longer duration of antibiotic treatment (>7d), compared to standard duration of antibiotic treatment (≤7d), improve clinical outcomes?
allPracticeChanges.category: In hospitalised adults with stroke associated pneumonia (isc
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In hospitalised adults with SAP (ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke; non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset, uncertainty remains regarding the effect of antibiotic treatment duration on clinical outcomes following acute stroke. Consequently, no evidence-based recommendations can currently be made. Please refer to the expert consensus statement below.

allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: In patients with SAP, we suggest initiating empirical antibiotic therapy in accordance with local or regional protocols, with primary reference to recommendations for aspiration pneumonia, targeting aerobic Gram-negative bacilli and Gram-positive cocci. Even in the presence of dysphagia or confirmed aspiration, extended antimicrobial treatment is not justified. Where relevant risk factors exist, empirical therapy should include coverage for Pseudomonas spp. For pneumonia developing more than 7 days after stroke onset, the group suggests following local or regional HAP protocols.

allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: In patients with SAP, we suggest initiating empiric antibiotic therapy as early as possible, ideally within a few hours of clinical diagnosis. Where feasible, the group also suggests performing routine microbiological diagnostics (e.g., sputum cultures) prior to starting antibiotic treatment to enable subsequent targeted antibiotic therapy based on pathogen identification.

allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: In patients with SAP, we suggest that adjunctive measures, such as cough-assist devices or breathing therapies, may be considered on an individual basis within an interdisciplinary stroke unit setting, although they are not part of standard treatment. These interventions may be particularly beneficial in patients with relevant comorbidities, such as COPD.

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 1: In people with aphasia after stroke is a higher dose of SLT (⩾20 hours) compared to a lower dose of SLT (< 20 hours) associated with greater improvements in language, communication, or quality of life?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In people with aphasia post-stroke, we recommend high dose SLT interventions (⩾20 hours) rather than lower dose SLT (< 20 hours) should be offered.
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In people with aphasia after stroke is a higher dose of SLT (⩾20 hours) compared to a lower dose of SLT (< 20 hours) associated with greater improvements in language, communication, or quality of life?

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 2: In people with aphasia after stroke is a higher intensity of SLT (⩾3 hours per week) compared to a lower intensity of SLT (< 3 hours per week) associated with greater improvements in language, communication or quality of life?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In people with aphasia post-stroke, we suggest high intensity SLT (⩾3 hours per week) rather than lower intensity should be offered.
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In people with aphasia after stroke is a higher intensity of SLT (⩾3 hours per week) compared to a lower intensity of SLT (< 3 hours per week) associated with greater improvements in language, communication or quality of life?

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 3: In people with aphasia after stroke is a higher frequency of SLT (⩾4 days per week) compared to a lower frequency of SLT (< 4 days per week) associated with greater improvements in language, communication or quality of life?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In people with aphasia post-stroke, we suggest high frequency SLT (⩾4 days per week) should be offered rather than lower frequency SLT (< 4 days per week).
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In people with aphasia after stroke is a higher frequency of SLT (⩾4 days per week) compared to a lower frequency of SLT (< 4 days per week) associated with greater improvements in language, communication or quality of life?

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 4a: In people with aphasia after stroke is digitally-delivered SLT (using telerehabilitation, virtual reality therapist or similar) compared to usual in-person SLT associated with similar improvements in language, communication or quality of life?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In people with aphasia after stroke, we suggest using either in-person or digitally-delivered SLT

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 4b: In people with aphasia after stroke is in-person SLT plus digital augmentation (using computer or tablet-based software, virtual reality or similar) compared to usual in-person SLT associated with greater improvements in language, communication or quality of life?
