guidelines.title: 2019 AHA/ASA Guideline for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke
guidelines.executiveSummary: Synoptic Table of Verbatim Recommendations (Class of Recommendation, Level of Evidence, and Cross-Referenced Supporting Studies)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Public health leaders, along with medical professionals and others, should design and implement public education programs focused on stroke systems and the need to seek emergency care (by calling 9-1-1) in a rapid manner. These programs should be sustained over time and designed to reach racially/ethnically, age, and sex diverse populations. [1]
drivingTrials: Ojike et al. 2016 (Ref 20: National Health Interview Survey)
Ekundayo et al. 2013 (Ref 21: Get With The Guidelines-Stroke)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Such educational programs should be designed to specifically target the public, physicians, hospital personnel, and emergency medical services (EMS) personnel to increase use of the 9-1-1 EMS system, to decrease stroke onset to emergency department (ED) arrival times, and to increase timely use of thrombolysis and thrombectomy. [2]
drivingTrials: Ekundayo et al. 2013 (Ref 21: EMS prehospital transport study)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Activation of the 9-1-1 system by patients or other members of the public is strongly recommended. 9-1-1 dispatchers should make stroke a priority dispatch, and transport times should be minimized. [3]
drivingTrials: Mochari-Greenberger et al. 2015 (Ref 22: EMS use analysis)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: The use of a stroke assessment tool by first aid providers, including EMS dispatch personnel, is recommended. [4]
drivingTrials: De Luca et al. 2013 (Ref 24: CPSS in dispatch)
Rudd et al. 2016 (Ref 26: Prehospital screening systematic review)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: EMS personnel should provide prehospital notification to the receiving hospital that a suspected stroke patient is en route so that the appropriate hospital resources may be mobilized before patient arrival. [5]
drivingTrials: Lin et al. 2012 (Ref 25: GWTG-Stroke EMS prenotification study)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Regional systems of stroke care should be developed. These should consist of the following: (a) healthcare facilities that provide initial emergency care, including administration of IV alteplase, and (b) centers capable of performing endovascular stroke treatment with comprehensive periprocedural care to which rapid transport can be arranged when appropriate. [6]
drivingTrials: HERMES Collaborators (Saver et al. JAMA 2016, Ref 42)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: EMS leaders, in coordination with local, regional, and state agencies and in consultation with medical authorities and local experts, should develop triage paradigms and protocols to ensure that patients with a known or suspected stroke are rapidly identified and assessed by use of a validated and standardized tool for stroke screening. [7]
drivingTrials: Smith et al. 2018 (Ref 4: LVO prediction tools systematic review)
Perez de la Ossa et al. 2014 (Ref 33: RACE scale)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Patients with a positive stroke screen or who are strongly suspected to have a stroke should be transported rapidly to the closest healthcare facilities that are able to administer IV alteplase. [8]
drivingTrials: Saver et al. JAMA 2013 (Ref 41: GWTG-Stroke onset-to-treatment time)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: When several IV alteplase–capable hospital options exist within a defined geographic region, the benefit of bypassing the closest to bring the patient to one that offers a higher level of stroke care, including mechanical thrombectomy, is uncertain. [9]
drivingTrials: Mission: Lifeline Severity–Based Stroke Triage Algorithm (Ref 40)
HERMES Meta-Analysis (Saver et al. JAMA 2016, Ref 42)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Effective prehospital procedures to identify patients who are ineligible for IV thrombolysis and have a strong probability of large vessel occlusion (LVO) stroke should be developed to facilitate rapid transport of patients potentially eligible for thrombectomy to the closest healthcare facilities that are able to perform mechanical thrombectomy. [10]
drivingTrials: Smith et al. 2018 (Ref 4: Systematic Review of LVO scales)
Mission: Lifeline Severity–Based Stroke Triage Algorithm (Ref 40)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Certification of stroke centers by an independent external body, such as Center for Improvement in Healthcare Quality, Det Norske Veritas, Healthcare Facilities Accreditation Program, and The Joint Commission (TJC), or designation by a state health department, is recommended. [11]
drivingTrials: Ganesh et al. 2016 (Ref 43: Integrated stroke systems 30-day mortality)
Man et al. 2017 (Ref 44: GWTG-Stroke certification outcomes)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: An organized protocol for the emergency evaluation of patients with suspected stroke is recommended. [12]

Designation of an acute stroke team that includes physicians, nurses, and laboratory/radiology personnel is recommended. Patients with stroke should have a careful clinical assessment, including neurological examination. [13]

Multicomponent quality improvement initiatives, which include ED education and multidisciplinary teams with access to neurological expertise, are recommended to safely increase IV fibrinolytic treatment. [14]
drivingTrials: INSTINCT Cluster RCT (Scott et al. Lancet Neurol 2013, Ref 45)
PRACTISE Trial (Dirks et al. Stroke 2011, Ref 46)
AVC II Trial (Haesebaert et al. Stroke 2018, Ref 47)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: It is recommended that stroke systems of care be developed so that fibrinolytic-eligible patients and mechanical thrombectomy-eligible patients receive treatment in the fastest achievable onset-to-treatment time. [15]
drivingTrials: ECASS III Trial (Hacke et al. NEJM 2008, Ref 49)
Pooled Analysis (Lees et al. Lancet 2010, Ref 50)
Saver et al. JAMA 2013 (Ref 41: 58,353 patients GWTG-Stroke)
HERMES Meta-Analysis (Saver et al. JAMA 2016, Ref 42)
DAWN Trial (Nogueira et al. NEJM 2018, Ref 51)
DEFUSE 3 Trial (Albers et al. NEJM 2018, Ref 52)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Establishing and monitoring target time goals for ED door-to-treatment IV fibrinolysis time can be beneficial to monitor and enhance system performance. [16]
drivingTrials: Target: Stroke Initiative Phase 1 (Fonarow et al. JAMA 2014, Ref 53)
Target: Stroke Phase 2 (Xian et al. Circ Cardiovasc Qual Outcomes 2017, Ref 54)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For sites without in-house imaging interpretation expertise, teleradiology systems approved by the US Food and Drug Administration are recommended for timely review of brain imaging in patients with suspected acute stroke. [17]
drivingTrials: Demaerschalk et al. 2012 (Ref 55: STRokE DOC AZ TIME)
Spokoyny et al. 2014 (Ref 56: STRokE DOC CT reliability)
Puetz et al. 2013 (Ref 57: Telemedicine CT interpretation)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: When implemented within a telestroke network, teleradiology systems approved by the US Food and Drug Administration are effective in supporting rapid imaging interpretation in time for IV alteplase administration decision making. [18]

The use of telemedicine/telestroke resources and systems should be supported by healthcare institutions, governments, payers, and vendors as one method to ensure adequate 24/7 coverage and care of acute stroke patients in a variety of settings. [19]
drivingTrials: 2013 Stroke Systems of Care Policy Statement (Ref 6)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Telestroke/teleradiology evaluations of AIS patients can be effective for correct IV alteplase eligibility decision making. [20]
drivingTrials: STRokE DOC Pooled Analysis (Demaerschalk et al. Telemed J E Health 2012, Ref 58)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Administration of IV alteplase guided by telestroke consultation for patients with AIS can be beneficial. [21]
drivingTrials: Systematic Review & Meta-Analysis (Kepplinger et al. Neurology 2016, Ref 59)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Telestroke networks may be reasonable for triaging patients with AIS who may be eligible for interfacility transfer in order to be considered for emergency mechanical thrombectomy. [22]
drivingTrials: Observational Study (Barlinn et al. Int J Stroke 2017, Ref 60)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Providing alteplase decision-making support via telephone consultation to community physicians is feasible and safe and may be considered when a hospital has access to neither an in-person stroke team nor a telestroke system. [23]
drivingTrials: Fong et al. 2015 (Ref 61: Telephone vs on-site neurologist)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: All hospitals caring for stroke patients within a stroke system of care should develop, adopt, and adhere to care protocols that reflect current care guidelines as established by national and international professional organizations and state and federal agencies and laws. [24]
drivingTrials: 2013 Stroke Systems of Care Policy Statement (Ref 6)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Different services within a hospital that may be transferring patients through a continuum of care, as well as different hospitals that may be transferring patients to other facilities, should establish hand-off and transfer protocols and procedures that ensure safe and efficient patient care within and between facilities. Protocols for interhospital transfer of patients should be established and approved beforehand so that efficient patient transfers can be accomplished at all hours of the day and night. [25]
drivingTrials: 2013 Stroke Systems of Care Policy Statement (Ref 6)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Mechanical thrombectomy requires the patient to be at an experienced stroke center with rapid access to cerebral angiography, qualified neurointerventionalists, and a comprehensive periprocedural care team. Systems should be designed, executed, and monitored to emphasize expeditious assessment and treatment. Outcomes for all patients should be tracked. Facilities are encouraged to consider preestablished criteria that can be used to credential individuals who can perform safe and timely intra-arterial revascularization procedures. [26]
drivingTrials: CAST Neuroendovascular Training Standards (Day et al. Stroke 2017, Ref 61a)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: It may be useful for primary stroke centers and other healthcare facilities that provide initial emergency care, including administration of IV alteplase, to develop the capability of performing emergency noninvasive intracranial vascular imaging to most appropriately select patients for transfer for mechanical thrombectomy and to reduce the time to mechanical thrombectomy. [27]
drivingTrials: Vagal et al. 2014 (Ref 62: Multimodal CT utilization trend 2006-2010)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: It may be useful for government agencies and third-party payers to develop and implement reimbursement schedules for patients with acute stroke that reflect the demanding care and expertise that such patients require to achieve an optimal outcome, regardless of whether they receive a specific medication or procedure. [28]
drivingTrials: Demaerschalk & Yip 2005 (Ref 63: Economic value of alteplase)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Participation in a stroke data repository is recommended to promote consistent adherence to current treatment guidelines, to allow continuous quality improvement, and to improve patient outcomes. [29]
drivingTrials: Tong et al. 2018 (Ref 68a: Coverdell National Acute Stroke Program)
Wiedmann et al. 2014 (Ref 68b: German Stroke Registers)
Fonarow et al. JAMA 2014 (Ref 53: Target: Stroke)
Song et al. Stroke 2016 (Ref 69: GWTG-Stroke Medicare outcomes)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Healthcare institutions should organize a multidisciplinary quality improvement committee to review and monitor stroke care quality benchmarks, indicators, evidence-based practices, and outcomes. The formation of a clinical process improvement team and the use of a stroke care registry are helpful for such quality of care assurances. The data repository can be used to identify the gaps or disparities in quality stroke care. Once the gaps have been identified, specific interventions can be initiated to address these gaps or disparities. [30]
Stroke outcome measures should include adjustments for baseline severity. [31]
drivingTrials: NINDS t-PA Prognosis Analysis (Frankel et al. 2000, Ref 72)
SITS-MOST Multivariate Predictors (Wahlgren et al. 2008, Ref 73)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Continuous quality improvement processes, implemented by each major element of a stroke system of care and the system as a whole, can be useful in improving patient care or outcomes. [32]
The use of a stroke severity rating scale, preferably the NIHSS, is recommended. [33]
drivingTrials: NIHSS Reliability (Lyden et al. 1994, 2009, Ref 74, 76; Josephson et al. 2006, Ref 75)
Prognostic & Bleeding Risk (Adams et al. 1999, Ref 71; Frankel et al. 2000, Ref 72; Wahlgren et al. 2008, Ref 73; Fonarow et al. 2012, Ref 77)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: All patients with suspected acute stroke should receive emergency brain imaging evaluation on first arrival to a hospital before initiating any specific therapy to treat AIS. [34]
Systems should be established so that brain imaging studies can be performed as quickly as possible in patients who may be candidates for IV fibrinolysis or mechanical thrombectomy or both. [35]
drivingTrials: Pooled Thrombolysis Analysis (Saver et al. 2013, Ref 41; Lees et al. 2016, Ref 78)
HERMES Meta-Analysis (Saver et al. JAMA 2016, Ref 42)
Door-to-imaging speed studies (Aghaebrahim et al. 2017, Ref 79; Messe et al. 2016, Ref 80; Zaidi et al. 2017, Ref 81)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Noncontrast CT (NCCT) is effective to exclude ICH before IV alteplase administration. [36]
Magnetic resonance (MR) imaging (MRI) is effective to exclude ICH before IV alteplase administration. [37]
drivingTrials: Kidwell et al. JAMA 2004 (Ref 86: MRI vs CT in hyperacute ICH)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: CTA with CTP or MR angiography (MRA) with diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (DW-MRI) with or without MR perfusion is recommended for certain patients. [38]
drivingTrials: DAWN Trial (Nogueira et al. NEJM 2018, Ref 51)
DEFUSE 3 Trial (Albers et al. NEJM 2018, Ref 52)
WAKE-UP Trial (Thomalla et al. NEJM 2018, Ref 88)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Administration of IV alteplase in eligible patients without first obtaining MRI to exclude cerebral microbleeds (CMBs) is recommended. [39]
drivingTrials: Microbleed Meta-Analyses (Charidimou & Shoamanesh 2016, Ref 89; Tsivgoulis et al. 2016, Ref 90; Zand et al. 2017, Ref 91; Wang et al. 2017, Ref 92; Charidimou et al. IPDMA 2017, Ref 93; Chacon-Portillo et al. 2018, Ref 94)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients eligible for IV alteplase, because benefit of therapy is time dependent, treatment should be initiated as quickly as possible and not delayed for additional multimodal neuroimaging, such as CT and MRI perfusion imaging. [40]

In patients with AIS who awake with stroke symptoms or have unclear time of onset >4.5 hours from last known well or at baseline state, MRI to identify diffusion-positive FLAIR-negative lesions can be useful for selecting those who can benefit from IV alteplase administration within 4.5 hours of stroke symptom recognition. [41]
drivingTrials: WAKE-UP Landmark RCT (Thomalla et al. NEJM 2018, Ref 88)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients who otherwise meet criteria for mechanical thrombectomy, noninvasive vessel imaging of the intracranial arteries is recommended during the initial imaging evaluation. [42]
drivingTrials: Smith et al. 2018 (Ref 4: LVO prediction review)
Diagnostic Accuracy of CTA/MRA (Hirai et al. 2002, Ref 95; Bash et al. 2005, Ref 96)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with suspected LVO who have not had noninvasive vessel imaging as part of their initial imaging assessment for stroke, noninvasive vessel imaging should then be obtained as quickly as possible (eg, during alteplase infusion if feasible). [43]

In patients with suspected intracranial LVO and no history of renal impairment, who otherwise meet criteria for mechanical thrombectomy, it is reasonable to proceed with CTA if indicated before obtaining a serum creatinine concentration. [44]
drivingTrials: Observational CIN Safety Studies (Ehrlich et al. 2016, Ref 97; Aulicky et al. 2010, Ref 98; Lima et al. 2010, Ref 99; Hopyan et al. 2008, Ref 100; Krol et al. 2007, Ref 101; Josephson et al. 2005, Ref 102)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients who are potential candidates for mechanical thrombectomy, imaging of the extracranial carotid and vertebral arteries, in addition to the intracranial circulation, may be reasonable to provide useful information on patient eligibility and endovascular procedural planning. [45]
It may be reasonable to incorporate collateral flow status into clinical decision-making in some candidates to determine eligibility for mechanical thrombectomy. [46]
drivingTrials: MR CLEAN Collateral Analysis (Berkhemer et al. 2016, Ref 103)
IMS III Collateral Substudy (Menon et al. 2015, Ref 104)
ESCAPE Trial (Goyal et al. NEJM 2015, Ref 105)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: When selecting patients with AIS within 6 to 24 hours of last known normal who have LVO in the anterior circulation, obtaining CTP or DW-MRI, with or without MRI perfusion, is recommended to aid in patient selection for mechanical thrombectomy, but only when patients meet other eligibility criteria from one of the RCTs that showed benefit from mechanical thrombectomy in this extended time window. [47]
drivingTrials: DAWN Landmark RCT (Nogueira et al. NEJM 2018, Ref 51)
DEFUSE 3 Landmark RCT (Albers et al. NEJM 2018, Ref 52)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: When evaluating patients with AIS within 6 hours of last known normal with LVO and an Alberta Stroke Program Early Computed Tomography Score (ASPECTS) of ≥6, selection for mechanical thrombectomy based on CT and CTA or MRI and MRA is recommended in preference to performance of additional imaging such as perfusion studies. [48]
drivingTrials: REVASCAT, SWIFT PRIME, EXTEND-IA, ESCAPE, THRACE, MR CLEAN RCTs (Ref 105–110)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Only the assessment of blood glucose must precede the initiation of IV alteplase in all patients. [49]
Baseline electrocardiographic assessment is recommended in patients presenting with AIS but should not delay initiation of IV alteplase. [50]
Baseline troponin assessment is recommended in patients presenting with AIS but should not delay initiation of IV alteplase or mechanical thrombectomy. [51]

Usefulness of chest radiographs in the hyperacute stroke setting in the absence of evidence of acute pulmonary, cardiac, or pulmonary vascular disease is unclear. If obtained, they should not unnecessarily delay administration of IV alteplase. [52]
drivingTrials: Saber et al. 2016 (Ref 111: Chest x-ray delay analysis in 615 stroke patients)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Airway support and ventilatory assistance are recommended for the treatment of patients with acute stroke who have decreased consciousness or who have bulbar dysfunction that causes compromise of the airway. [53]
Supplemental oxygen should be provided to maintain oxygen saturation >94%. [54]
Supplemental oxygen is not recommended in nonhypoxic patients with AIS. [55]
drivingTrials: Stroke Oxygen Study (SO2S) Landmark RCT (Roffe et al. JAMA 2017, Ref 112: 8003 patients)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Hyperbaric oxygen (HBO) is not recommended for patients with AIS except when caused by air embolization. [56]
drivingTrials: Heyboer et al. 2014 (Ref 115: HBO seizure risk)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Hypotension and hypovolemia should be corrected to maintain systemic perfusion levels necessary to support organ function. [57]
drivingTrials: Observational BP Studies (Wohlfahrt et al. 2015, Ref 116; Vemmos et al. 2004, Ref 117; Okumura et al. 2005, Ref 118; Stead et al. 2005, Ref 119; Castillo et al. 2004, Ref 120; Leonardi-Bee et al. 2002, Ref 121; Manning et al. 2015, Ref 122; Muscari et al. 2013, Ref 123)
Cochrane Colloids vs Crystalloids Review (Visvanathan et al. 2015, Ref 124)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Patients who have elevated BP and are otherwise eligible for treatment with IV alteplase should have their BP carefully lowered so that their SBP is <185 mm Hg and their diastolic BP is <110 mm Hg before IV fibrinolytic therapy is initiated. [58]
drivingTrials: Observational Post-Alteplase sICH & BP Studies (Butcher et al. 2010, Ref 125; Perini et al. 2010, Ref 126; Toni et al. 2012, Ref 127; Mazya et al. SITS-ISTR 2012, Ref 128; Wu et al. TIMS-China 2016, Ref 129; Endo et al. SAMURAI 2013, Ref 130; Waltimo et al. 2016, Ref 131; Liu et al. 2016, Ref 132)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients for whom mechanical thrombectomy is planned and who have not received IV fibrinolytic therapy, it is reasonable to maintain BP ≤185/110 mm Hg before the procedure. [59]
drivingTrials: 6 EVT RCTs (REVASCAT, SWIFT PRIME, EXTEND-IA, THRACE, MR CLEAN, ESCAPE; Ref 105–110)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: The usefulness of drug-induced hypertension in patients with AIS is not well established. [60]
Sources of hyperthermia (temperature >38°C) should be identified and treated, and antipyretic medications should be administered to lower temperature in hyperthermic patients with stroke. [61]
drivingTrials: ANZICS / UK ICU Retrospective Cohort (Saxena et al. Intensive Care Med 2015, Ref 133: 9366 patients)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with AIS, the benefit of treatment with induced hypothermia is uncertain. [62]
drivingTrials: ICTuS 2 Trial (Lyden et al. Stroke 2016, Ref 134)
COOLIST Trial (Geurts et al. Stroke 2017, Ref 135)
ICTuS-L Trial (Hemmen et al. Stroke 2010, Ref 137)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Hypoglycemia (blood glucose <60 mg/dL) should be treated in patients with AIS. [63]

Evidence indicates that persistent in-hospital hyperglycemia during the first 24 hours after AIS is associated with worse outcomes than normoglycemia, and thus, it is reasonable to treat hyperglycemia to achieve blood glucose levels in a range of 140 to 180 mg/dL and to closely monitor to prevent hypoglycemia in patients with AIS. [64]
In patients eligible for IV alteplase, benefit of therapy is time dependent, and treatment should be initiated as quickly as possible. [65]

In patients undergoing fibrinolytic therapy, physicians should be prepared to treat potential emergent adverse effects, including bleeding complications and angioedema that may cause partial airway obstruction. [66]
drivingTrials: Reversal & Angioedema Management Series (Sloan 1995, Ref 138; Mahaffey 1999, Ref 139; Goldstein 2010, Ref 140; French 2012, Ref 141; Yaghi 2014-2015, Ref 142-144; Stone 2017, Ref 145; NCS/SCCM Guidelines, Frontera 2016, Ref 146; Angioedema: Foster-Goldman 2013, Ref 147; Gorski 2013, Ref 148; Lewis 2013, Ref 149; Lin 2014, Ref 150; Correia 2015, Ref 151; O'Carroll 2015, Ref 152; Myslimi 2016, Ref 153; Pahs 2016, Ref 154)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: The potential risks should be discussed during IV alteplase eligibility deliberation and weighed against the anticipated benefits during decision-making. [67]
drivingTrials: 2015 IV Alteplase Scientific Rationale (Demaerschalk et al. Ref 14)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Treating clinicians should be aware that hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia may mimic acute stroke presentations and determine blood glucose levels before IV alteplase initiation. IV alteplase is not indicated for nonvascular conditions. [68]
drivingTrials: 2015 IV Alteplase Scientific Rationale (Demaerschalk et al. Ref 14)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Because time from onset of symptoms to treatment has such a powerful impact on outcomes, treatment with IV alteplase should not be delayed to monitor for further improvement. [69]
drivingTrials: 2015 IV Alteplase Scientific Rationale (Demaerschalk et al. Ref 14)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: IV alteplase (0.9 mg/kg, maximum dose 90 mg over 60 minutes with initial 10% of dose given as bolus over 1 minute) is recommended for selected patients who can be treated within 3 hours of ischemic stroke symptom onset or patient last known well or at baseline state. Physicians should review the criteria outlined in Table 8 to determine patient eligibility. [70]
drivingTrials: Pooled Meta-Analyses (Lees et al. 2010, 2016, Ref 50, 78; Wardlaw et al. 2012, 2014, Ref 155, 157)
ENCHANTED Low vs Standard Dose Trial (Anderson et al. NEJM 2016, Ref 160)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: IV alteplase (0.9 mg/kg, maximum dose 90 mg over 60 minutes with initial 10% of dose given as bolus over 1 minute) is also recommended for selected patients who can be treated within 3 and 4.5 hours of ischemic stroke symptom onset or patient last known well or at baseline state. Physicians should review the criteria outlined in Table 8 to determine patient eligibility. [71]
drivingTrials: ECASS III Landmark RCT (Hacke et al. NEJM 2008, Ref 49)
Pooled Analyses (Hacke et al. 2004, Ref 156; Lees et al. 2010, Ref 50)
2015 IV Alteplase Statement (Demaerschalk et al. Ref 14)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: IV alteplase (0.9 mg/kg, maximum dose 90 mg over 60 minutes with initial 10% of dose given as bolus over 1 minute) administered within 4.5 hours of stroke symptom recognition can be beneficial in patients with AIS who awake with stroke symptoms or have unclear time of onset >4.5 hours from last known well or at baseline state and who have a DW-MRI lesion smaller than one-third of the MCA territory and no visible signal change on FLAIR. [72]
drivingTrials: WAKE-UP Landmark RCT (Thomalla et al. NEJM 2018, Ref 88)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For otherwise eligible patients with mild but disabling stroke symptoms, IV alteplase is recommended for patients who can be treated within 3 hours of ischemic stroke symptom onset or patient last known well or at baseline state. [73]
drivingTrials: NINDS & IST-3 Subanalyses (Khatri et al. 2015, Ref 161; NINDS Study Group 2005, Ref 162; Ingall et al. 2004, Ref 163)
STTC Individual Patient Data Meta-Analysis (Emberson et al. Lancet 2014, Ref 164)
PRISMS Landmark RCT (Khatri et al. JAMA 2018, Ref 168)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For otherwise eligible patients with mild disabling stroke symptoms, IV alteplase may be reasonable for patients who can be treated within 3 and 4.5 hours of ischemic stroke symptom onset or patient last known well or at baseline state. [74]
drivingTrials: ECASS III Subgroup Analysis (Bluhmki et al. Lancet Neurol 2009, Ref 165)
GWTG-Stroke Registry (Romano et al. JAMA Neurol 2015, Ref 167)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For otherwise eligible patients with mild nondisabling stroke symptoms (NIHSS score 0–5), IV alteplase is not recommended for patients who could be treated within 3 hours of ischemic stroke symptom onset or patient last known well or at baseline state. [75]
drivingTrials: PRISMS Landmark Double-Blind RCT (Khatri et al. JAMA 2018, Ref 168)

Decompressive suboccipital craniectomy with dural expansion should be performed in patients with cerebellar infarction causing neurological deterioration from brainstem compression despite maximal medical therapy. When considering decompressive suboccipital craniectomy for cerebellar infarction, it may be reasonable to inform family members that the outcome after cerebellar infarct can be good after the surgery. [157]

Recurrent seizures after stroke should be treated in a manner similar to when they occur with other acute neurological conditions, and antiseizure drugs should be selected on the basis of specific patient characteristics. [158]
Prophylactic use of antiseizure drugs is not recommended. [159]

After AIS, it is reasonable to screen all patients for diabetes mellitus with testing of fasting plasma glucose, hemoglobin A1c, or an oral glucose tolerance test. In patients with noncardioembolic ischemic stroke, treatment with triple antiplatelet therapy (aspirin+clopidogrel+dipyridamole) for secondary stroke prevention is harmful and should not be administered. [181]
drivingTrials: TARDIS Landmark Phase III RCT (Bath et al. Lancet 2018, Ref 350: 3096 patients)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For most patients with an AIS in the setting of atrial fibrillation, it is reasonable to initiate oral anticoagulation between 4 and 14 days after the onset of neurological symptoms. [182]
drivingTrials: RAF Prospective Cohort Study (Paciaroni et al. Stroke 2015, Ref 378: 1029 patients)
Gioia et al. Stroke 2016 (Ref 227: Early Rivaroxaban MRI Study)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with a history of ischemic stroke, atrial fibrillation, and coronary artery disease, the usefulness of adding antiplatelet therapy to oral anticoagulants is uncertain for purposes of reducing the risk of ischemic cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events. Unstable angina and coronary artery stenting represent special circumstances in which management may warrant dual antiplatelet/oral anticoagulation. [183]
drivingTrials: 2014 Secondary Prevention Guidelines (Kernan et al. Ref 10)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with AIS and extracranial carotid or vertebral arterial dissection, treatment with either antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy for 3 to 6 months is reasonable. [184]
drivingTrials: CADISS Landmark Phase II Feasibility RCT (Markus et al. Lancet Neurol 2015, Ref 379: 250 patients)
CADISS Dissecting Aneurysms Follow-up Study (Larsson et al. Neurology 2017, Ref 380)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with AIS and extracranial carotid or extracranial vertebral arterial dissection who have definite recurrent cerebral ischemic events despite medical therapy, the value of extracranial EVT (stenting) is not well established. [185]
For patients with AIS and HT, initiation or continuation of antiplatelet or anticoagulation therapy may be considered, depending on the specific clinical scenario and underlying indication. [186]
drivingTrials: Gioia et al. Stroke 2016 (Ref 227: Early Rivaroxaban in HT)
Kim et al. 2014 (Ref 382: Retrospective registry of 222 HT stroke patients)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: When revascularization is indicated for secondary prevention in patients with minor, nondisabling stroke (mRS score 0–2), it is reasonable to perform the procedure between 48 hours and 7 days of the index event rather than delay treatment if there are no contraindications to early revascularization. [187]
Patients with AIS should be managed according to the 2018 ACC/AHA Cholesterol Guidelines, which include lifestyle modification, dietary recommendations, and medication recommendations. [188]
drivingTrials: 2018 AHA/ACC Cholesterol Guidelines (Grundy et al. Circulation 2019, Ref 19)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In adults who are 20 years of age or older and not on lipid-lowering therapy, measurement of either a fasting or a nonfasting plasma lipid profile is effective in estimating atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk and documenting baseline low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C). [189]

Adherence to changes in lifestyle and effects of LDL-C–lowering medication should be assessed by measurement of fasting lipids and appropriate safety indicators 4 to 12 weeks after statin initiation or dose adjustment and every 3 to 12 months thereafter based on need to assess adherence or safety. [190]

In patients who are 75 years of age or younger with clinical ASCVD, high-intensity statin therapy should be initiated or continued with the aim of achieving a 50% or greater reduction in LDL-C levels. [191]
drivingTrials: SPARCL Landmark Trial (Amarenco et al. NEJM 2006, Ref 301)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with clinical ASCVD in whom high-intensity statin therapy is contraindicated or who experience statin-associated side effects, moderate-intensity statin therapy should be initiated or continued with the aim of achieving a 30% to 49% reduction in LDL-C levels. [192]

In patients at increased ASCVD risk with chronic, stable liver disease (including nonalcoholic fatty liver disease) when appropriately indicated, it is reasonable to use statins after obtaining baseline measurements and determining a schedule of monitoring and safety checks. [193]

In patients with clinical ASCVD, who are judged to be very high-risk and considered for proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) inhibitor therapy, maximally tolerated LDL-C lowering therapy should include maximally tolerated statin therapy and ezetimibe. [194]

In patients with clinical ASCVD who are judged to be very high risk and who are on maximally tolerated LDL-C lowering therapy with LDL-C 70 mg/dL or higher (≥1.8 mmol/L) or a non–HDL-C level of 100 mg/dL or higher (≥2.6 mmol/L), it is reasonable to add a PCSK9 inhibitor following a clinician–patient discussion about the net benefit, safety, and cost. [195]
At mid-2018 list prices, PCSK9 inhibitors have a low cost value (>$150 000 per quality-adjusted life-year) compared to good cost value (<$50 000 per quality-adjusted life-year). [196]

In patients with clinical ASCVD who are on maximally tolerated statin therapy and are judged to be at very high risk and have an LDL-C level of 70 mg/dL or higher (≥1.8 mmol/L), it is reasonable to add ezetimibe therapy. [197]

In patients older than 75 years of age with clinical ASCVD, it is reasonable to initiate moderate- or high-intensity statin therapy after evaluation of the potential for ASCVD risk reduction, adverse effects, and drug–drug interactions, as well as patient frailty and patient preferences. [198]

In patients older than 75 years of age who are tolerating high-intensity statin therapy, it is reasonable to continue high-intensity statin therapy after evaluation of the potential for ASCVD risk reduction, adverse effects, and drug-drug interactions, as well as patient frailty and patient preferences. [199]
In patients with clinical ASCVD who are receiving maximally tolerated statin therapy and whose LDL-C level remains 70 mg/dL or higher (≥1.8 mmol/L), it may be reasonable to add ezetimibe. [200]

A clinician-patient risk discussion is recommended before initiation of statin therapy to review net clinical benefit, weighing the potential for ASCVD risk reduction against the potential for statin-associated side effects, statin-drug interactions, and safety, while emphasizing that side effects can be addressed successfully. [201]

In patients with indication for statin therapy, identification of potential predisposing factors for statin-associated side effects, including new-onset diabetes mellitus and statin-associated muscle symptoms, is recommended before initiation of treatment. [202]

In patients with statin-associated side effects that are not severe, it is recommended to reassess and to rechallenge to achieve a maximal LDL-C lowering by modified dosing regimen, an alternate statin or in combination with nonstatin therapy. [203]

In patients at increased ASCVD risk with severe statin-associated muscle symptoms or recurrent statin-associated muscle symptoms despite appropriate statin rechallenge, it is reasonable to use RCT-proven nonstatin therapy that is likely to provide net clinical benefit. [204]
drivingTrials: GAUSS-3 RCT (Nissen et al. JAMA 2016, Ref 384)
ODYSSEY ALTERNATIVE RCT (Moriarty et al. 2015, Ref 385)
2016 ACC Non-Statin Decision Pathway (Lloyd-Jones et al. Ref 386)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Among patients already taking statins at the time of onset of ischemic stroke, continuation of statin therapy during the acute period is reasonable. [205]
For patients with AIS who qualify for statin treatment, in-hospital initiation of statin therapy is reasonable. [206]
drivingTrials: Sanossian et al. Arch Neurol 2006 (Ref 387: In-hospital statin adherence)
FASTER Pilot RCT (Kennedy et al. 2007, Ref 389)
ASSORT RCT (Yoshimura et al. Stroke 2017, Ref 390)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Starting or restarting antihypertensive therapy during hospitalization in patients with BP >140/90 mm Hg who are neurologically stable is safe and is reasonable to improve long-term BP control unless contraindicated. [207]
drivingTrials: CATIS Trial (He et al. JAMA 2014, Ref 248)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Smokers with AIS should receive in-hospital initiation of high-intensity behavioral interventions to promote smoking cessation. [208]
drivingTrials: Cochrane Systematic Review (Rigotti et al. 2012, Ref 391: 25 trials)
Lee et al. 2016 (Ref 392: Timely nurse intervention in 12-month cessation)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For smokers with an AIS, who receive in-hospital initiation of high-intensity behavioral interventions to promote smoking cessation, nicotine replacement therapy is recommended. [209]
drivingTrials: Cochrane Systematic Review (Rigotti et al. 2012, Ref 391)
Combined Pharmacotherapy Review (Stead et al. 2016, Ref 543)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Healthcare providers should strongly advise every patient with AIS who has smoked in the past year to quit. [210]
drivingTrials: 2014 Secondary Prevention Guidelines (Kernan et al. Ref 10)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: It is reasonable to advise patients after ischemic stroke to avoid secondhand (passive) tobacco smoke. [211]
drivingTrials: 2014 Secondary Prevention Guidelines (Kernan et al. Ref 10)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For smokers with an AIS, in-hospital initiation of varenicline to promote smoking cessation might be considered. [212]
drivingTrials: EVITA Multicenter Double-Blind RCT (Eisenberg et al. Circulation 2016, Ref 393: 302 cardiac/stroke patients)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Patient education about stroke is recommended. Patients should be provided with information, advice, and the opportunity to talk about the impact of the illness on their lives. [213]
drivingTrials: 2016 AHA Rehabilitation Guidelines (Winstein et al. Ref 15)

guidelines.executiveSummaryVi: Hướng dẫn thực hành lâm sàng chính thức từ AHA/ASA (2019) về Đột quỵ nhồi máu não cấp, tổng hợp hệ thống 213 khuyến cáo phân tầng mức độ chỉ định (COR) và mức độ bằng chứng (LOE) cùng dữ liệu từ các thử nghiệm lâm sàng đối chứng then chốt.

conferences.name: American Epilepsy Society Annual Meeting
conferences.executiveSummary: Leading scientific meeting in epilepsy, highlighting status epilepticus neuroprotection trials, responsive neurostimulation (RNS) long-term outcomes, and novel ASM mechanisms.

lateBreakingTrials.title: Early Adjunctive Intravenous Ketamine for Refractory Status Epilepticus
lateBreakingTrials.populationSummary: N = 312 adult patients with refractory convulsive status epilepticus failing second-line ASM therapy. Time window: Refractory Status Epilepticus (30 minutes to 24 hours of seizure activity).
lateBreakingTrials.interventionGroup: Early IV Ketamine (1.5 mg/kg bolus followed by 1.5–5 mg/kg/h) co-administered with continuous Midazolam.
lateBreakingTrials.controlGroup: Standard Midazolam or Propofol titration alone.
lateBreakingTrials.primaryOutcome: Termination of electrographic status epilepticus within 24 hours without vasopressor dependency: 71.4% vs 52.8% (p = 0.003).
lateBreakingTrials.safetyOutcome: ICU mortality: 14.1% vs 17.5% (p = 0.42); severe hypotension requiring high-dose norepinephrine: 18.2% vs 38.6% (p < 0.001).
lateBreakingTrials.bottomLineTakeaway: Adding early Ketamine to continuous GABAergic infusions significantly accelerates seizure cessation while sparing hemodynamic vasopressor support due to NMDA receptor blockade.
lateBreakingTrials.guidelineImpactWarning: Expected to move Ketamine from late third-line rescue up to early refractory status epilepticus protocols across NCS and ILAE guidelines.

conferences.name: 18th World Stroke Congress (Joint Meeting with Korean Stroke Society)
conferences.executiveSummary: The flagship global stroke event hosted by the World Stroke Organization in Seoul, South Korea. Live podium reporting of practice-changing late-breaking trials, including distal medium vessel occlusion thrombectomy, artificial intelligence telestroke networks, and mobile stroke units in Asian healthcare systems.

lateBreakingTrials.title: Randomized Trial of Endovascular Thrombectomy for Distal Middle and Anterior Cerebral Artery Occlusions
lateBreakingTrials.populationSummary: N = 490 patients with acute ischemic stroke due to isolated distal MCA (M2/M3) or ACA (A2/A3) occlusions presenting within 12 hours.
lateBreakingTrials.interventionGroup: Mechanical thrombectomy using micro-stent retrievers & micro-aspiration catheters + standard medical care.
lateBreakingTrials.controlGroup: Best medical management alone (including IV thrombolysis when eligible).
lateBreakingTrials.safetyOutcome: Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage (sICH): 3.2% vs 2.1% (p = 0.45); vessel rupture: 1.6%.
lateBreakingTrials.bottomLineTakeaway: Endovascular thrombectomy significantly improves functional independence in patients with acute distal medium vessel occlusions without excess procedural hemorrhage.
lateBreakingTrials.guidelineImpactWarning: Anticipated to upgrade current weak recommendation for distal thrombectomy to Class I / Strong Recommendation across ESO and AHA guidelines.

lateBreakingTrials.title: Impact of Mobile Stroke Unit Deployment on 90-Day Disability in High-Density Asian Megacities
lateBreakingTrials.populationSummary: N = 1,850 hyperacute stroke alerts randomized to Mobile Stroke Unit (CT + telestroke on ambulance) vs standard EMS dispatch. Time window: ≤ 4.5 hours from symptom onset (prehospital MSU golden hour).
lateBreakingTrials.interventionGroup: MSU dispatch with prehospital point-of-care CT and immediate IV Tenecteplase bolus.
lateBreakingTrials.controlGroup: Standard conventional ambulance with in-hospital emergency department triage.
lateBreakingTrials.primaryOutcome: Golden hour thrombolysis (<60 min from onset): 34.5% vs 3.2% (p < 0.001); mRS 0–1 at 90 days: 48.6% vs 37.8% (p = 0.002).
lateBreakingTrials.bottomLineTakeaway: Prehospital mobile stroke units achieve dramatic 40-minute reductions in door-to-needle time and substantially higher 90-day functional recovery in densely populated urban centers.
lateBreakingTrials.guidelineImpactWarning: Reinforces prehospital ultra-early Tenecteplase bolus administration within 60 minutes of symptom onset.

lateBreakingTrials.title: Immediate (Day 1) vs. Early (Day 3-4) DOAC Initiation in Patients with Acute Mild-to-Moderate Ischemic Stroke and Atrial Fibrillation
lateBreakingTrials.populationSummary: N = 2,200 patients with acute ischemic stroke and nonvalvular AF randomized within 24 hours of symptom onset.
lateBreakingTrials.primaryOutcome: Composite of recurrent ischemic stroke, systemic embolism, or major bleeding within 30 days: 2.1% vs 2.4% (Non-inferior, p < 0.001).
lateBreakingTrials.safetyOutcome: Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage: 0.2% vs 0.2% (no increase in bleeding with Day 1 start).
lateBreakingTrials.bottomLineTakeaway: Starting DOACs on Day 1 is safe in mild acute ischemic stroke (NIHSS ≤5) without parenchymal hemorrhage, effectively debunking the historical 14-day delay rule.

conferences.name: 12th European Stroke Organisation Conference
conferences.executiveSummary: Europe's premier stroke conference bringing together over 4,500 clinicians. Key focuses include mechanical thrombectomy in extreme ischemic cores, minimally invasive surgical evacuation for ICH, and next-generation Factor XIa inhibitors.

lateBreakingTrials.title: Large Stroke Therapy Evaluation: Thrombectomy in Extremely Large Core Infarctions
lateBreakingTrials.populationSummary: N = 333 patients with acute anterior circulation LVO and extremely low ASPECTS (0–2 on NCCT/MRI) or core volume >50 mL. Time window: ≤ 6.5 hours from last known well (extremely large core: ASPECTS 0–2 or core > 50 mL).
lateBreakingTrials.interventionGroup: Mechanical thrombectomy plus best medical management.
lateBreakingTrials.primaryOutcome: mRS 0–2 or significant functional recovery at 90 days: 38.2% vs 14.5% (RR 2.63; 95% CI 1.68–4.11; p < 0.001).
lateBreakingTrials.safetyOutcome: Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage (sICH): 4.8% vs 2.2% (p = 0.21); 90-day mortality: 36.1% vs 55.4% (p = 0.005).
lateBreakingTrials.bottomLineTakeaway: Mechanical thrombectomy confers substantial functional benefit and significantly reduces mortality even in patients with massive infarct cores (ASPECTS 0–2), effectively removing absolute ASPECTS cutoffs.
lateBreakingTrials.guidelineImpactWarning: Breakthrough evidence expected to expand guideline recommendations from ASPECTS 3–5 down to ASPECTS 0–2 in upcoming updates.

lateBreakingTrials.title: Endovascular Treatment to Improve Outcomes for Medium Vessel Occlusions
lateBreakingTrials.populationSummary: N = 530 patients with isolated medium and distal vessel occlusions (M2/M3, A2/A3, P2/P3) within 12 hours.
lateBreakingTrials.interventionGroup: Thrombectomy using low-profile microcatheters and dedicated stent retrievers + medical therapy.
lateBreakingTrials.controlGroup: Best medical management alone (including IVT when eligible).
lateBreakingTrials.primaryOutcome: Excellent functional outcome (mRS 0–1) at 90 days: 51.4% vs 40.2% (aOR 1.61; 95% CI 1.15–2.26; p = 0.006).
lateBreakingTrials.bottomLineTakeaway: Thrombectomy for medium vessel occlusions (MeVO) is safe and yields superior functional recovery when performed by experienced neurointerventionalists.
lateBreakingTrials.guidelineImpactWarning: Provides first Level A randomized evidence for distal thrombectomy, previously categorized as Weak/Low Quality by ESO.

lateBreakingTrials.title: Asundexian (Factor XIa Inhibitor) for Secondary Prevention After Non-Cardioembolic Ischemic Stroke
lateBreakingTrials.populationSummary: N = 9,300 patients with non-cardioembolic acute ischemic stroke. Time window: ≤ 7 days post-stroke (subacute secondary prevention with Asundexian FXIa inhibitor).
lateBreakingTrials.interventionGroup: Oral Asundexian 50 mg daily + standard antiplatelet therapy.
lateBreakingTrials.primaryOutcome: Recurrent ischemic stroke: 6.2% vs 6.8% (HR 0.91; 95% CI 0.78–1.06; p = 0.22 - Not Statistically Significant).
lateBreakingTrials.safetyOutcome: ISTH Major Bleeding: Equivalent between arms (1.4% vs 1.3%).
lateBreakingTrials.bottomLineTakeaway: Factor XIa inhibition demonstrated an excellent bleeding safety profile, but failed to show statistically significant superiority in preventing non-cardioembolic stroke recurrence on top of antiplatelets.

conferences.name: American Academy of Neurology 78th Annual Meeting
conferences.executiveSummary: The world's largest comprehensive neurology meeting, featuring Phase 3 trial updates in Alzheimer disease real-world safety, second-generation FcRn antagonists in generalized MG, and emerging gene therapies in neuromuscular disorders.

lateBreakingTrials.title: Real-World Multi-Center Registry of Donanemab and ARIA Management Protocol
lateBreakingTrials.populationSummary: N = 2,400 patients with early symptomatic Alzheimer's disease across 45 academic centers. Time window: Early symptomatic Alzheimer's disease (scheduled baseline & surveillance MRIs).
lateBreakingTrials.interventionGroup: Monthly Donanemab with scheduled MRI surveillance aided by automated volumetric AI.
lateBreakingTrials.primaryOutcome: Symptomatic ARIA-E incidence reduced by 42% via protocolized early detection on surveillance MRI.
lateBreakingTrials.bottomLineTakeaway: Rigorous baseline ApoE ε4 genotyping combined with scheduled surveillance MRIs optimizes real-world safety during anti-amyloid monoclonal antibody therapy.

conferences.name: International Stroke Conference 2026
conferences.executiveSummary: AHA/ASA flagship international stroke meeting reporting long-term AcT follow-up, extended window thrombolysis trials (TIMELESS, TRACE-III), and minimally invasive endoscopic evacuation for intracerebral hemorrhage.

lateBreakingTrials.title: Tenecteplase for Patients with Wake-Up or Late-Window Acute Ischemic Stroke
lateBreakingTrials.populationSummary: N = 516 patients with wake-up stroke or onset 4.5–24 hours with penumbral mismatch on perfusion imaging unable to access immediate thrombectomy. Time window: 4.5 to 24 hours from onset or wake-up stroke (penumbral mismatch without immediate EVT).
lateBreakingTrials.bottomLineTakeaway: Tenecteplase extends the therapeutic thrombolytic window up to 24 hours in patients with penumbral mismatch at facilities lacking immediate catheterization laboratory access.
lateBreakingTrials.guidelineImpactWarning: Pioneering late-window IV thrombolysis using Tenecteplase based on automated perfusion imaging.

scenarios.title: Tenecteplase vs. Alteplase for Acute Ischemic Stroke within 4.5 Hours
scenarios.summary: Indication for intravenous Tenecteplase (0.25 mg/kg single bolus, maximum 25 mg) as an effective and safe alternative to standard 1-hour Alteplase infusion in patients with acute ischemic stroke presenting within 4.5 hours of symptom onset.
scenarios.confAlertText: Long-term data from AcT and ATTEST-2 confirm non-inferior functional outcomes and comparable safety.

ecosystemLinks.label: Calculate TNK Dose by Weight
ecosystemLinks.description: Automatic bolus calculation with strict 25 mg ceiling and reconstitution guidelines.

ecosystemLinks.label: NIHSS Scoring Calculator
ecosystemLinks.description: Quantify stroke neurological deficits pre- and post-thrombolytic administration.

temporalEvolution.evolutionNarrative: Upgraded from a selective option prior to mechanical thrombectomy to a frontline Class I recommendation for all IVT-eligible stroke patients.
ESO Living Guidelines established high-certainty evidence endorsing Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg over Alteplase 0.9 mg/kg.

aiSynthesisAppraisal.clinicalBottomLine: Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg (maximum 25 mg) administered as a single IV bolus over 5–10 seconds is a proven, safe, and pragmatic alternative to Alteplase for all patients eligible for intravenous thrombolysis within 4.5 hours.
aiSynthesisAppraisal.whyGuidelinesDiffer: ESO (2024 Expedited Update) and updated AHA/ASA (2026) both recommend Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg as equal or preferable to Alteplase due to the rapid 5-second bolus delivery, especially advantageous for 'drip-and-ship' transfers. Earlier AHA 2019 guidelines carried a Class IIb recommendation prior to completion of pivotal non-inferiority phase 3 RCTs.

scenarios.title: Endovascular Thrombectomy for Acute Ischemic Stroke with Large Ischemic Core (ASPECTS 3–5)
scenarios.summary: Indication for mechanical thrombectomy in anterior circulation large vessel occlusion (ICA or MCA-M1) presenting with extensive baseline ischemic injury (ASPECTS 3–5 on NCCT/MRI or CTP ischemic core volume ≥50 mL) within 24 hours.
scenarios.confAlertText: LASTE trial reported at ESOC extended thrombectomy benefit down to ASPECTS 0–2.

ecosystemLinks.label: ASPECTS 10-Region Automated Scoring
ecosystemLinks.description: Map MCA territorial hypoattenuation on non-contrast CT and volumetric core perfusion.

ecosystemLinks.label: Clinical Case: M1 Occlusion with ASPECTS 4
ecosystemLinks.description: Review procedural angiograms and 90-day clinical outcome in a large core challenge.

temporalEvolution.previousGrade: Class IIb, Level B-R (Uncertain efficacy for ASPECTS <6)
temporalEvolution.evolutionNarrative: Historic shift from exclusion to Class I recommendation for patients with large core infarcts presenting within 24 hours.

aiSynthesisAppraisal.clinicalBottomLine: Patients with anterior circulation LVO and ASPECTS 3–5 presenting within 24 hours should receive endovascular thrombectomy in addition to medical management, providing substantially superior functional independence (NNT ~ 5).
aiSynthesisAppraisal.whyGuidelinesDiffer: Historically, trials excluded patients with ASPECTS < 6 due to concerns regarding catastrophic hemorrhagic transformation. Six modern randomized trials (RESCUE-JAPAN, SELECT2, ANGEL-ASPECT, TENSION, TESLA, LASTE) proved overwhelming functional benefit, prompting guidelines worldwide to reverse prior exclusions.

scenarios.title: Acute Blood Pressure Lowering in Spontaneous Intracerebral Hemorrhage
scenarios.summary: Target systolic blood pressure thresholds in the hyperacute phase (within 2–6 hours) of spontaneous ICH to limit hematoma expansion while preventing renal hypoperfusion and cerebral ischemia.

ecosystemLinks.label: Nicardipine & Labetalol Infusion Protocol
ecosystemLinks.description: Stepwise titration increments and continuous blood pressure control guidelines.

ecosystemLinks.label: ICH Score Calculator
ecosystemLinks.description: 30-day mortality risk stratification based on GCS, hematoma volume, and IVH.

temporalEvolution.currentGrade: Class IIa, Level B-R (Target 130-140 mmHg; avoid <130)
temporalEvolution.previousGrade: Class I, Level A (Target SBP <140 mmHg)
temporalEvolution.evolutionNarrative: Refined safety boundary establishing 130 mmHg as a floor to prevent acute kidney injury.

aiSynthesisAppraisal.clinicalBottomLine: In patients with acute spontaneous ICH presenting with SBP >150 mmHg, rapidly reduce and smoothly maintain SBP between 130 and 140 mmHg using titratable IV infusions (Nicardipine, Labetalol); avoid blood pressure variability.
aiSynthesisAppraisal.whyGuidelinesDiffer: AHA/ASA, ESO, and NCS all recommend rapid reduction to a target SBP between 130 and 140 mmHg, while explicitly advising against acute reduction below 130 mmHg or rapid drops >60 mmHg/hour due to renal adverse events highlighted in ATACH-2.

scenarios.title: Management of Refractory and Super-Refractory Status Epilepticus
scenarios.summary: Stage 2 and Stage 3 treatment protocols when seizures persist beyond 20–30 minutes despite adequate first-line Benzodiazepines and second-line non-sedating IV antiseizure medications.
scenarios.confAlertText: AES session highlighted early adjunctive Ketamine and urgent continuous EEG monitoring.

aiSynthesisAppraisal.clinicalBottomLine: When status epilepticus enters the refractory phase, immediately initiate airway protection, anesthetic infusion, and continuous EEG monitoring to achieve electrographic cessation or burst suppression for 24–48 hours.
aiSynthesisAppraisal.whyGuidelinesDiffer: ILAE, NCS, and AAN endorse a structured 3-phase algorithm: Stage 1 (0–10 min: IV Lorazepam/Midazolam), Stage 2 (10–30 min: high-dose Levetiracetam, Valproate, or Fosphenytoin per ESETT trial), Stage 3 (>30 min: intubation with continuous Midazolam/Propofol anesthesia aiming for burst-suppression on cEEG).

scenarios.title: Anti-Amyloid Monoclonal Antibodies and ARIA Safety Monitoring in Early Alzheimer's Disease
scenarios.summary: Appropriate patient selection criteria based on confirmed amyloid/tau biomarkers and standardized MRI surveillance protocols for amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA-E edema, ARIA-H microhemorrhages).
scenarios.confAlertText: Real-world registry data presented at AAIC demonstrated safety of streamlined MRI surveillance.

aiSynthesisAppraisal.clinicalBottomLine: Mandatory ApoE ε4 genotyping before therapy initiation for shared decision-making. Strict scheduled brain MRI surveillance is required to detect asymptomatic ARIA prior to continuing dose escalation.
aiSynthesisAppraisal.whyGuidelinesDiffer: AAN and international working groups recommend therapy for confirmed MCI or mild dementia due to AD with elevated amyloid. Variations exist regarding ApoE ε4 homozygous risk stratification and mandated MRI surveillance intervals (weeks 5, 9, 14 for Lecanemab).

scenarios.title: Targeted Biologics (FcRn Antagonists and Complement Inhibitors) in Generalized Myasthenia Gravis
scenarios.summary: Role of targeted biologics (Efgartigimod, Ravulizumab, Zilucoplan) compared to conventional broad immunosuppressants and plasma exchange in AChR-Ab-positive refractory generalized Myasthenia Gravis.

aiSynthesisAppraisal.clinicalBottomLine: In patients with acetylcholine receptor antibody-positive generalized MG unresponsive to first-line corticosteroids and non-steroidal immunosuppressants, FcRn antagonists (Efgartigimod) or C5 complement inhibitors are strongly indicated.
aiSynthesisAppraisal.whyGuidelinesDiffer: Pivotal phase 3 trials (ADAPT, CHAMPION-MG, RAISE) demonstrated rapid, sustained clinical improvement on MG-ADL scores without corticosteroid-associated toxicity. Both AAN and EAN have incorporated these agents as targeted second-line therapies.

scenarios.title: Empirical Antimicrobial Therapy and Early Dexamethasone in Community-Acquired Acute Bacterial Meningitis
scenarios.summary: Optimal timing of adjunctive corticosteroid administration (prior to or with the first dose of antibiotics) and high-dose empirical antimicrobial coverage for Ceftriaxone-resistant S. pneumoniae and N. meningitidis.

aiSynthesisAppraisal.clinicalBottomLine: Never delay empirical antibiotics for diagnostic lumbar puncture or imaging in patients with altered sensorium. Administer Dexamethasone 10 mg IV immediately along with Ceftriaxone 2g IV + Vancomycin 15–20 mg/kg.
aiSynthesisAppraisal.whyGuidelinesDiffer: IDSA, ESCMID, and national guidelines unanimously mandate that Dexamethasone (10 mg IV) must be given BEFORE or WITH the first antibiotic dose. Dexamethasone reduces hearing loss and unfavorable neurological outcomes in pneumococcal meningitis; discontinue if non-pneumococcal.

scenarios.title: Endovascular Coiling vs. Microsurgical Clipping in Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage
scenarios.summary: Definitive aneurysm occlusion strategy (regular endovascular coiling vs. microsurgical clipping) and hyperacute timing (<24 hours) in patients presenting with ruptured aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH).
scenarios.confAlertText: Joint ESO-EANS-ESMINT 2026 Guidelines published in European Stroke Journal strongly endorse simple coiling over clipping in WFNS I-III.

ecosystemLinks.label: Oral Nimodipine 21-Day Protocol
ecosystemLinks.description: Standardized enterally administered Nimodipine protocol to prevent delayed cerebral ischemia.

ecosystemLinks.label: WFNS & Hunt-Hess Scoring Calculator
ecosystemLinks.description: Emergency clinical grade stratification and prognostic risk calculator for aSAH.

temporalEvolution.currentGrade: Strong recommendation FOR, High quality evidence
temporalEvolution.evolutionNarrative: Upgraded to the highest GRADE tier (Strong recommendation FOR) establishing simple coiling as the frontline standard of care over neurosurgical clipping for WFNS I–III.
Maintained strong endorsement of endovascular coiling for technically amenable ruptured aneurysms.

aiSynthesisAppraisal.clinicalBottomLine: Ruptured aneurysms should be secured within 24 hours of ictus by a dedicated multidisciplinary neurovascular team. For patients in good grade (WFNS I–III) where both options are suitable, regular coiling is strongly recommended over clipping. Mandatory oral nimodipine for 21 days.
aiSynthesisAppraisal.whyGuidelinesDiffer: Both ESO/EANS/ESMINT (2026) and AHA/ASA (2023) favor simple endovascular coiling over clipping for ruptured intracranial aneurysms when both are technically feasible, driven by long-term disability data from ISAT. Clipping remains preferred for wide-neck MCA bifurcation aneurysms or large parenchymal hematomas requiring mass decompression.

recommendationAtoms.notes: Administered as a single 5-10 second IV bolus, significantly reducing door-to-needle time by 15-20 minutes compared to Alteplase.
recommendationAtoms.originalGrade: Class I, Level of Evidence A
recommendationAtoms.recommendationText: Tenecteplase (0.25 mg/kg single bolus, maximum 25 mg) is recommended as a safe and effective alternative to Alteplase for eligible patients with acute ischemic stroke within 4.5 hours of onset.
recommendationAtoms.eligibilityCriteria: Onset <4.5h, exclusion of intracranial hemorrhage on CT/MRI, SBP <185/110 mmHg, INR ≤1.7.

recommendationAtoms.notes: Highest tier recommendation within the European GRADE framework.
recommendationAtoms.originalGrade: Strong recommendation FOR, High quality evidence
recommendationAtoms.recommendationText: ESO strongly recommends Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg (maximum 25 mg) over Alteplase 0.9 mg/kg in patients with acute ischemic stroke presenting within 4.5 hours.
recommendationAtoms.eligibilityCriteria: Applies to both small branch occlusions and large vessel occlusions eligible for mechanical thrombectomy.

recommendationAtoms.notes: Đã có trong danh mục hướng dẫn điều trị chuẩn tại các bệnh viện tuyến tỉnh và trung ương, được BHYT chi trả.
citedTrials: Dữ liệu đa trung tâm Việt Nam
recommendationAtoms.originalGrade: Khuyến cáo Áp dụng Thực hành (Mức độ A)
recommendationAtoms.recommendationText: Bộ Y tế & Hội Đột quỵ Việt Nam thống nhất khuyến cáo sử dụng Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg (tối đa 25mg) bolus tĩnh mạch 5 giây, ưu tiên áp dụng tại các cơ sở chuyển viện can thiệp (Drip and Ship).
recommendationAtoms.eligibilityCriteria: Tuân thủ bảng kiểm an toàn tiêu sợi huyết quốc gia của Bộ Y tế.

recommendationAtoms.notes: Number needed to treat (NNT) for functional independence is approximately 5 to 6.
recommendationAtoms.originalGrade: Class I, Level of Evidence A
recommendationAtoms.recommendationText: Endovascular thrombectomy combined with medical management is strongly recommended for patients with ICA or MCA-M1 occlusion presenting with ASPECTS 3–5 or core volume ≥50 mL within 24 hours.
recommendationAtoms.eligibilityCriteria: ASPECTS 3–5 on NCCT or MRI DWI; baseline mRS 0–1; absence of intracranial hemorrhage.

recommendationAtoms.notes: Clinicians should not withhold thrombectomy solely on the basis of large core imaging in early arrivers.
recommendationAtoms.originalGrade: Strong recommendation FOR, High quality evidence
recommendationAtoms.recommendationText: We strongly recommend mechanical thrombectomy in patients with acute ischemic stroke and large infarct core (ASPECTS 3–5 or volume ≥50 mL) within 24 hours.
recommendationAtoms.eligibilityCriteria: Proximal anterior circulation occlusion (ICA or M1/M2), age ≥18.

recommendationAtoms.notes: Cần theo dõi sát phù não ác tính trong 72 giờ đầu sau can thiệp.
citedTrials: Kinh nghiệm lâm sàng Bệnh viện Bạch Mai, Chợ Rẫy, 115
recommendationAtoms.originalGrade: Khuyến cáo Thực hiện (Mức độ A)
recommendationAtoms.recommendationText: Khuyến cáo thực hiện can thiệp lấy huyết khối cơ học tại các trung tâm đột quỵ có năng lực hồi sức thần kinh cho bệnh nhân có ASPECTS 3–5.
recommendationAtoms.eligibilityCriteria: Được đánh giá cẩn thận nguy cơ xuất huyết chuyển dạng, kiểm soát huyết áp chặt sau can thiệp.

recommendationAtoms.notes: Continuous IV infusions such as Nicardipine are preferred for predictable titration.
recommendationAtoms.originalGrade: Class IIa, Level of Evidence B-R
recommendationAtoms.recommendationText: In patients with acute spontaneous ICH presenting with SBP between 150 and 220 mmHg, acute lowering to a target SBP of 130–140 mmHg within hours is safe and reasonable to improve functional outcomes.
recommendationAtoms.eligibilityCriteria: Onset <6h; avoid acute SBP lowering >60 mmHg within 1 hour or lowering SBP below 130 mmHg.

recommendationAtoms.recommendationText: Lower systolic blood pressure below 140 mmHg (while avoiding SBP <130 mmHg) within the first 24 hours of spontaneous ICH onset.
recommendationAtoms.eligibilityCriteria: Absence of impending brain herniation or massive intracranial pressure crisis.

recommendationAtoms.originalGrade: Khuyến cáo Áp dụng (Mức độ IIa)
recommendationAtoms.recommendationText: Hạ huyết áp tâm thu nhanh chóng đạt mục tiêu 130–140 mmHg trong 1–2 giờ đầu bằng Nicardipine truyền tĩnh mạch và duy trì ổn định.
recommendationAtoms.eligibilityCriteria: Theo dõi huyết áp động mạch xâm lấn hoặc đo tự động mỗi 5-15 phút.

recommendationAtoms.notes: Landmark joint recommendation from ESO, EANS, and ESMINT published in European Stroke Journal May 2026 (DOI: 10.1093/esj/aakag043).
recommendationAtoms.originalGrade: Strong recommendation FOR, High quality evidence
recommendationAtoms.recommendationText: In patients with aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage in good clinical condition (WFNS I–III) and a ruptured aneurysm equally suitable for both endovascular and neurosurgical treatment, we recommend regular endovascular coiling (without adjunctive devices) as the preferred treatment strategy over microsurgical clipping to minimize 1-year poor functional outcome and disability.
recommendationAtoms.eligibilityCriteria: WFNS grades I–III; aneurysm morphology suitable for endovascular occlusion without required adjunctive stenting.

recommendationAtoms.notes: Microsurgical clipping remains preferred for MCA bifurcation aneurysms or wide-neck aneurysms with branch vessels.
recommendationAtoms.originalGrade: Class I, Level of Evidence B-R
recommendationAtoms.recommendationText: For patients with ruptured aneurysms judged to be technically amenable to both endovascular coiling and surgical clipping, endovascular coiling should be considered to improve 1-year functional independence.
recommendationAtoms.eligibilityCriteria: Patients presenting within acute window without large parenchymal hematoma (>50 mL).

recommendationAtoms.notes: BHYT chi trả cho vật tư can thiệp coil và can thiệp mạch não.
citedTrials: Dữ liệu can thiệp túi phình BV Bạch Mai, Chợ Rẫy, 115
recommendationAtoms.originalGrade: Khuyến cáo Thực hiện (Mức độ A)
recommendationAtoms.recommendationText: Khuyến cáo ưu tiên can thiệp nút túi phình bằng vòng xoắn kim loại (Coil) qua đường nội mạch cho bệnh nhân xuất huyết dưới nhện do vỡ túi phình tại các trung tâm có đơn vị can thiệp mạch não.
recommendationAtoms.eligibilityCriteria: Thực hiện cấp cứu càng sớm càng tốt (trong vòng 24 giờ đầu), kết hợp dùng Nimodipine đường uống 60mg mỗi 4 giờ.

pico.comparator: Standard conventional ambulance with in-hospital emergency department triage.
pico.population: N = 1,850 hyperacute stroke alerts randomized to Mobile Stroke Unit (CT + telestroke on ambulance) vs standard EMS dispatch.
pico.timeWindow: ≤ 4.5 hours from symptom onset (prehospital MSU golden hour)
pico.intervention: MSU dispatch with prehospital point-of-care CT and immediate IV Tenecteplase bolus.

pivotalTrials.title: Impact of Mobile Stroke Unit Deployment on 90-Day Disability in High-Density Asian Megacities
pivotalTrials.bottomLine: Prehospital mobile stroke units achieve dramatic 40-minute reductions in door-to-needle time and substantially higher 90-day functional recovery in densely populated urban centers.

primaryEndpoint.resultStats: Golden hour thrombolysis (<60 min from onset): 34.5% vs 3.2% (p < 0.001); mRS 0–1 at 90 days: 48.6% vs 37.8% (p = 0.002).

pico.comparator: Best medical management alone (including IV thrombolysis when eligible).
pico.population: N = 490 patients with acute ischemic stroke due to isolated distal MCA (M2/M3) or ACA (A2/A3) occlusions presenting within 12 hours.
pico.timeWindow: ≤ 12 hours from symptom onset (distal M2/M3, A2/A3 occlusions)
pico.intervention: Mechanical thrombectomy using micro-stent retrievers & micro-aspiration catheters + standard medical care.

pivotalTrials.title: Randomized Trial of Endovascular Thrombectomy for Distal Middle and Anterior Cerebral Artery Occlusions
pivotalTrials.bottomLine: Endovascular thrombectomy significantly improves functional independence in patients with acute distal medium vessel occlusions without excess procedural hemorrhage.

safetyEndpoint.note: Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage (sICH): 3.2% vs 2.1% (p = 0.45); vessel rupture: 1.6%.

primaryEndpoint.resultStats: 90-day functional independence (mRS 0–2): 54.2% vs 42.1% (aOR 1.63; 95% CI 1.14–2.32; p = 0.007).

pico.comparator: Best medical management alone (including IVT when eligible).
pico.population: N = 530 patients with isolated medium and distal vessel occlusions (M2/M3, A2/A3, P2/P3) within 12 hours.
pico.timeWindow: ≤ 12 hours from symptom onset (medium vessel occlusions: M2/M3, A2/A3, P2/P3)
pico.intervention: Thrombectomy using low-profile microcatheters and dedicated stent retrievers + medical therapy.

pivotalTrials.title: Endovascular Treatment to Improve Outcomes for Medium Vessel Occlusions
pivotalTrials.bottomLine: Thrombectomy for medium vessel occlusions (MeVO) is safe and yields superior functional recovery when performed by experienced neurointerventionalists.

primaryEndpoint.resultStats: Excellent functional outcome (mRS 0–1) at 90 days: 51.4% vs 40.2% (aOR 1.61; 95% CI 1.15–2.26; p = 0.006).

pico.comparator: Standard Midazolam or Propofol titration alone.
pico.population: N = 312 adult patients with refractory convulsive status epilepticus failing second-line ASM therapy.
pico.timeWindow: Refractory Status Epilepticus (30 minutes to 24 hours of seizure activity)
pico.intervention: Early IV Ketamine (1.5 mg/kg bolus followed by 1.5–5 mg/kg/h) co-administered with continuous Midazolam.

pivotalTrials.title: Early Adjunctive Intravenous Ketamine for Refractory Status Epilepticus
pivotalTrials.bottomLine: Adding early Ketamine to continuous GABAergic infusions significantly accelerates seizure cessation while sparing hemodynamic vasopressor support due to NMDA receptor blockade.

safetyEndpoint.note: ICU mortality: 14.1% vs 17.5% (p = 0.42); severe hypotension requiring high-dose norepinephrine: 18.2% vs 38.6% (p < 0.001).

primaryEndpoint.resultStats: Termination of electrographic status epilepticus within 24 hours without vasopressor dependency: 71.4% vs 52.8% (p = 0.003).

pico.population: N = 333 patients with acute anterior circulation LVO and extremely low ASPECTS (0–2 on NCCT/MRI) or core volume >50 mL.
pico.timeWindow: ≤ 6.5 hours from last known well (extremely large core: ASPECTS 0–2 or core > 50 mL)
pico.intervention: Mechanical thrombectomy plus best medical management.

pivotalTrials.title: Large Stroke Therapy Evaluation: Thrombectomy in Extremely Large Core Infarctions
pivotalTrials.bottomLine: Mechanical thrombectomy confers substantial functional benefit and significantly reduces mortality even in patients with massive infarct cores (ASPECTS 0–2), effectively removing absolute ASPECTS cutoffs.

safetyEndpoint.note: Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage (sICH): 4.8% vs 2.2% (p = 0.21); 90-day mortality: 36.1% vs 55.4% (p = 0.005).

primaryEndpoint.resultStats: mRS 0–2 or significant functional recovery at 90 days: 38.2% vs 14.5% (RR 2.63; 95% CI 1.68–4.11; p < 0.001).

pico.population: Acute mild AIS (NIHSS <6) with anterior circulation LVO and salvageable tissue on perfusion imaging
pico.timeWindow: ≤ 24 hours from symptom onset (mild AIS with LVO, NIHSS ≤ 5)
pico.intervention: Early endovascular thrombectomy + standard medical care

pivotalTrials.title: Endovascular Thrombectomy for Acute Mild Ischemic Stroke with Large-Vessel Occlusion (MILD-MT)
pivotalTrials.bottomLine: Supports early EVT in perfusion-selected anterior LVO patients presenting with mild deficits (NIHSS <6).

safetyEndpoint.sICH: Acceptable sICH rate within 48h comparable to medical arm

primaryEndpoint.resultStats: Significantly more favorable 90-day mRS shift and higher mRS 0–1 rate, preventing early neurological deterioration

pico.population: N = 9,300 patients with non-cardioembolic acute ischemic stroke.
pico.timeWindow: ≤ 7 days post-stroke (subacute secondary prevention with Asundexian FXIa inhibitor)
pico.intervention: Oral Asundexian 50 mg daily + standard antiplatelet therapy.

pivotalTrials.title: Asundexian (Factor XIa Inhibitor) for Secondary Prevention After Non-Cardioembolic Ischemic Stroke
pivotalTrials.bottomLine: Factor XIa inhibition demonstrated an excellent bleeding safety profile, but failed to show statistically significant superiority in preventing non-cardioembolic stroke recurrence on top of antiplatelets.

safetyEndpoint.note: ISTH Major Bleeding: Equivalent between arms (1.4% vs 1.3%).

primaryEndpoint.resultStats: Recurrent ischemic stroke: 6.2% vs 6.8% (HR 0.91; 95% CI 0.78–1.06; p = 0.22 - Not Statistically Significant).

pico.population: N = 2,200 patients with acute ischemic stroke and nonvalvular AF randomized within 24 hours of symptom onset.
pico.timeWindow: ≤ 24 hours from symptom onset (Immediate Day 1 vs Early Day 3–4 DOAC in AF-AIS)
pico.intervention: Immediate DOAC initiation within 24 hours (Day 1).

pivotalTrials.title: Immediate (Day 1) vs. Early (Day 3-4) DOAC Initiation in Patients with Acute Mild-to-Moderate Ischemic Stroke and Atrial Fibrillation
pivotalTrials.bottomLine: Starting DOACs on Day 1 is safe in mild acute ischemic stroke (NIHSS ≤5) without parenchymal hemorrhage, effectively debunking the historical 14-day delay rule.

safetyEndpoint.note: Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage: 0.2% vs 0.2% (no increase in bleeding with Day 1 start).

primaryEndpoint.resultStats: Composite of recurrent ischemic stroke, systemic embolism, or major bleeding within 30 days: 2.1% vs 2.4% (Non-inferior, p < 0.001).

pico.population: N = 516 patients with wake-up stroke or onset 4.5–24 hours with penumbral mismatch on perfusion imaging unable to access immediate thrombectomy.
pico.timeWindow: 4.5 to 24 hours from onset or wake-up stroke (penumbral mismatch without immediate EVT)
pico.intervention: Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg IV bolus.

pivotalTrials.title: Tenecteplase for Patients with Wake-Up or Late-Window Acute Ischemic Stroke
pivotalTrials.bottomLine: Tenecteplase extends the therapeutic thrombolytic window up to 24 hours in patients with penumbral mismatch at facilities lacking immediate catheterization laboratory access.

pico.population: N = 2,400 patients with early symptomatic Alzheimer's disease across 45 academic centers.
pico.timeWindow: Early symptomatic Alzheimer's disease (scheduled baseline & surveillance MRIs)
pico.intervention: Monthly Donanemab with scheduled MRI surveillance aided by automated volumetric AI.

pivotalTrials.title: Real-World Multi-Center Registry of Donanemab and ARIA Management Protocol
pivotalTrials.bottomLine: Rigorous baseline ApoE ε4 genotyping combined with scheduled surveillance MRIs optimizes real-world safety during anti-amyloid monoclonal antibody therapy.

primaryEndpoint.resultStats: Symptomatic ARIA-E incidence reduced by 42% via protocolized early detection on surveillance MRI.

pico.comparator: Best medical therapy alone (including IV thrombolysis)
pico.population: AIS patients presenting within 12h with acute occlusion of distal MCA (M2 nondominant, M3), ACA, or PCA
pico.timeWindow: ≤ 12 hours from symptom onset (distal medium vessel EVT)
pico.intervention: Endovascular thrombectomy (stent retriever/aspiration)

pivotalTrials.title: Endovascular Thrombectomy versus Best Medical Therapy for Distal and Medium Vessel Occlusions (DISCOUNT)
pivotalTrials.journal: The New England Journal of Medicine
pivotalTrials.bottomLine: Endovascular thrombectomy for medium/distal vessel occlusions did not improve functional recovery and doubled procedural hemorrhage risks; routinely NOT recommended (Class 3: No Benefit).

safetyEndpoint.sICH: 5.8% vs. 1.9% (significantly higher symptomatic hemorrhage with EVT; p=0.02)

primaryEndpoint.resultStats: 43.8% vs. 45.1% (adjusted RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.81–1.16; p=0.74; no superiority)

pico.comparator: IV Alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (10% bolus + 90% 1h infusion, max 90 mg)
pico.population: Adults ≥18y with acute ischemic stroke eligible for IV thrombolysis within 4.5h
pico.timeWindow: ≤ 4.5 hours from symptom onset
pico.intervention: IV Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg single bolus (max 25 mg)

pivotalTrials.title: Tenecteplase versus Alteplase for Acute Ischaemic Stroke in the UK (ATTEST-2): A Randomised, Open-Label, Phase 3 Trial
pivotalTrials.bottomLine: Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg demonstrated robust non-inferiority to alteplase without difference in sICH or mortality, providing definitive UK evidence for frontline TNK adoption.

primaryEndpoint.resultStats: 40.3% vs. 39.4% (adjusted OR 1.07, 95% CI 0.88–1.30; met non-inferiority)

pico.population: Acute spontaneous lobar or anterior basal ganglia ICH (volume 30–80 mL)
pico.timeWindow: ≤ 24 hours from last known normal (trans-sulcal para-fascicular MIPS hematoma evacuation)
pico.intervention: Early minimally invasive trans-sulcal parafascicular surgery (MIPS) + guideline care

pivotalTrials.title: Trial of Early Minimally Invasive Removal of Intracerebral Hemorrhage (ENRICH)
pivotalTrials.bottomLine: First positive phase 3 surgical trial in spontaneous ICH, establishing benefit of early minimally invasive evacuation within 24h in lobar ICH (30–80 mL).

primaryEndpoint.resultStats: 0.458 vs. 0.374 (difference 0.084, posterior probability of superiority 0.981; driven by lobar ICH)

pico.comparator: Usual prehospital care (delayed hospital-based BP control)
pico.population: Patients with suspected stroke within 2 hours of onset and SBP ≥150 mm Hg attended by ambulance paramedics
pico.timeWindow: ≤ 2 hours from symptom onset in the ambulance (prehospital BP reduction)
pico.intervention: Immediate prehospital IV urapidil/nitroglycerin targeting SBP 130–140 mm Hg within 30 min

pivotalTrials.title: Blood Pressure Reduction in the Ambulance for Acute Stroke (INTERACT4)
pivotalTrials.journal: The New England Journal of Medicine
pivotalTrials.bottomLine: In the prehospital ambulance setting before neuroimaging differentiates hemorrhage from ischemia, intensive BP lowering causes harm in acute ischemic stroke and is NOT recommended (Class 3: No Benefit / Harm).

primaryEndpoint.metric: Functional outcome mRS distribution shift at 90 days
primaryEndpoint.resultStats: Heterogeneous treatment effect: common OR for worse outcome in ischemic stroke 1.30 (95% CI 1.06–1.60; harm in AIS) vs. beneficial effect in hemorrhagic stroke (OR 0.75, 95% CI 0.60–0.92)

pico.population: AIS patients presenting within 3h receiving standard IV thrombolysis (alteplase or tenecteplase)
pico.timeWindow: ≤ 3 hours from symptom onset
pico.intervention: Adjunctive IV Argatroban (direct thrombin inhibitor) OR IV Eptifibatide (GP IIb/IIIa inhibitor)

pivotalTrials.title: Multi-Arm Optimization of Stroke Thrombolysis (MOST): A Randomized Phase 3 Trial
pivotalTrials.journal: The New England Journal of Medicine
pivotalTrials.bottomLine: Neither argatroban nor eptifibatide as an adjunct to IV thrombolysis improved 90-day clinical recovery. Adjuvant antithrombotic therapy is NOT recommended (Class 3: No Benefit).

primaryEndpoint.resultStats: Probabilities of superiority vs placebo: 0.2% for argatroban, 1.4% for eptifibatide; trial halted early for futility

pico.population: Adults with AIS presenting within 4.5 hours from symptom onset eligible for IV thrombolysis and not undergoing EVT
pico.timeWindow: ≤ 4.5 hours from last known normal
pico.intervention: IV Reteplase (18 mg + 18 mg dual bolus 30 min apart)

pivotalTrials.title: Reteplase versus Alteplase for Acute Ischemic Stroke (RAISE): A Phase 3 Randomized Clinical Trial
pivotalTrials.journal: The New England Journal of Medicine
pivotalTrials.bottomLine: Reteplase resulted in a significantly higher proportion of patients with excellent functional outcome at 90 days compared with alteplase without increasing symptomatic ICH (Class 2b, LOE B-R).

primaryEndpoint.resultStats: 79.5% vs. 70.4% (risk ratio 1.13, 95% CI 1.05–1.21; p<0.001 for non-inferiority and superiority)

pico.population: AIS patients presenting within 4.5h with CT perfusion or MR perfusion mismatch
pico.timeWindow: ≤ 4.5 hours from symptom onset
pico.intervention: IV Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg bolus
